I was there from the very beginning of it all, though I didn’t know it at the time. I had left my ordinary life behind to follow John the Baptist out in the wilderness by the Jordan River. The air was dry and hot, carrying the scent of dust and river water, the crowds pressing close as John preached with a voice like thunder rolling over the hills. His camel-hair cloak scratched against his skin, his eyes burned with holy urgency. “Repent,” he would cry, “for the kingdom of heaven is at hand!” I felt the weight of my own sins heavy on my shoulders as I watched others go down into the muddy waters—and I sensed, dimly, that the weight was the whole point, that something was wrong in me that washing alone could not reach.

Then one ordinary afternoon, the sun glinting off the river, a man approached from the north. He was ordinary in appearance—strong build from years of labor, dust on His sandals, a quiet steadiness in His step. John saw Him and stopped everything. His voice cracked with reverence as he pointed: “Behold, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world!” Those words pierced me like a spear. I had carried lambs to the altar; I knew what a lamb was for. A lamb was for a sinner who could not pay his own debt, a life given in the place of another. I did not grasp it then, but a seed was planted in me that hour—that this Man had come not only to preach the kingdom but to carry away the very thing that had bowed my shoulders. My heart leaped, a strange warmth spreading through my chest. Who was this Jesus of Nazareth? I had to know.

Two of us—Andrew and I—left John that day and began following Jesus at a distance. The path was rocky, the sun warm on our backs. He turned, saw us, and asked gently, “What are you seeking?” His voice was calm, deep, like still water after a storm. We stumbled over our words: “Rabbi, where are you staying?” He smiled, eyes full of knowing, and said, “Come and see.” We walked with Him to where He was staying as the sun dipped lower, painting the hills in gold and shadow. We sat with Him until the stars came out, talking deep into the night. I cannot remember every word, but I felt seen—truly seen—for the first time. His gaze held no judgment, only light and invitation. It struck me even then that I had not found Him so much as He had let Himself be found; He had turned and asked the first question, as if the seeking had begun on His side long before it began on mine. A fire kindled in my spirit, quiet but growing, as if something ancient and new was awakening inside me. That night, sleep came lightly; my mind hummed with possibility.

The next morning, Andrew found his brother Simon and brought him to Jesus. I stood close as Jesus looked at Simon—rough fisherman, broad shoulders, calloused hands—and said, “You are Simon the son of John. You shall be called Cephas,” which means Peter, the rock. I saw Simon’s face shift from surprise to something deeper, a mix of awe and uncertainty flickering in his eyes. We all felt it: this man named things not only as they were but as they would become. He looked at a wavering fisherman and called him rock, and I began to wonder whether this was how He meant to save us—not by finding finished men, but by laying hold of unfinished ones and remaking them into what they could never become on their own.

We traveled together then into Galilee. The roads wound through fields of grain and olive groves, the air sweet with ripening fruit. Jesus found Philip along the way. “Follow me,” He said simply. Philip’s face lit up like dawn breaking, and he hurried to tell Nathanael. I was there when Philip brought him. Nathanael was skeptical under the shade of a fig tree, wiping sweat from his brow. “Can anything good come out of Nazareth?” he muttered. But we went anyway, and I began to notice that the kingdom advanced this way—one person found, then sent to find another, the circle of the rescued widening with every step.

Jesus saw Nathanael approaching and called out, “Behold, an Israelite indeed, in whom there is no deceit!” Nathanael’s steps faltered. “How do you know me?” Jesus replied softly, yet with power, “Before Philip called you, when you were under the fig tree, I saw you.” The words hung in the warm air. I felt a shiver run down my spine, the hairs on my arms rising. How could He know? He had seen Nathanael before Nathanael had sought Him, known him before he was known. Nathanael dropped to his knees almost at once, voice trembling with wonder: “Rabbi, you are the Son of God! You are the King of Israel!” Jesus placed a hand on his shoulder, His touch steady and reassuring. “Because I said to you, ‘I saw you under the fig tree,’ do you believe? You will see greater things than these. Truly, truly, I say to you, you will see heaven opened, and the angels of God ascending and descending on the Son of Man.”

My own pulse quickened. The ground beneath my feet felt sacred, as if the veil between heaven and earth had thinned. A holy fear mixed with joy in my belly—like standing before a burning bush that did not consume. Heaven opened, He had said—the very heaven that sin had shut against us—and He Himself the ladder between earth and sky, the meeting place of God and man. If that was true, then He was the one thing we had always needed and never had.

The following day we went up to Cana for a wedding. The village buzzed with celebration: music drifting on the breeze, tables laden with bread and fish, laughter echoing off stone walls. Families in their finest robes, children darting between legs. Jesus’ mother was there, her face lined with care and wisdom. I watched her approach Him quietly amid the joy. “They have no wine,” she said. Jesus answered with tenderness but firmness, “Woman, what does this have to do with me? My hour has not yet come.” Yet she turned to the servants with calm trust: “Do whatever He tells you.” The word about His hour lodged in me; even in the middle of a feast He seemed to be measuring His steps toward some appointed time none of us could see.

Six stone jars stood nearby, massive and cool to the touch, used for purification rites. Each could hold twenty or thirty gallons. Jesus spoke to the servants, His voice clear above the crowd: “Fill the jars with water.” They obeyed, drawing from the well until water brimmed at the top, spilling slightly onto the dusty ground. Then, “Now draw some out and take it to the master of the feast.” It did not escape me, even then, that He began with the jars kept for washing away defilement, and turned what they held into the wine of gladness.

I held my breath, heart thudding against my ribs, as a servant carried the cup across the courtyard. The master tasted it—his eyes widened in delight. He pulled the bridegroom aside, voice loud with surprise: “Everyone serves the good wine first, and when people have drunk freely, then the poor wine. But you have kept the good wine until now!” The aroma reached me: rich, fragrant, better than any wine I had known. My hands shook as I realized what had happened. Water—plain, ordinary water—had become this. I looked at Jesus. He stood quietly, not seeking praise, His face peaceful in the lamplight.

Awe crashed over me like waves on the shore. My throat tightened, tears stung my eyes unbidden. This was glory revealed, not in thunder but in quiet abundance—and it was the abundance that undid me. The world’s joy always ran out and ended in the lesser thing; here was One who kept the best until last and poured it out freely on people who had done nothing to earn it. I began to suspect that whatever this Man had come to give, He would give like this: not grudgingly, not as wages owed to the deserving, but lavishly, beyond all reckoning. Faith took root deeper in my soul that night, like a seed in fertile soil after rain.

From Cana we went down to Capernaum by the sea. The journey was dusty, the lake sparkling blue in the distance. Jesus walked with that unhurried strength, and simply being in His presence made the road lighter. We stayed in a simple home near the shore, the sound of waves lapping stones a constant murmur. Evenings, we gathered as lamps flickered, casting warm shadows on the walls. His teachings sank into us: the kingdom breaking in now, among the ordinary. His words were like bread—nourishing, filling. I felt my old life peeling away, layer by layer, and I sensed that following Him would not leave me as He had found me; He meant to remake me, not merely improve me.

From Capernaum we made our way up to Jerusalem for the Passover. The road climbed steadily through the hills of Judea, the dust clinging to our sandals and the hems of our robes, turning them a pale gray. Olive groves gave way to rocky terraces planted with vines, and the air grew warmer as we drew nearer to the holy city. Jesus walked ahead with that same unhurried strength, His shoulders steady under the weight of His simple cloak. We were going up for the feast of the lamb’s blood—the night Israel had been spared because a death fell on a lamb in her place—and though I did not yet draw the line between the feast and the Man, the two were walking up to Jerusalem together.

As we approached, the city rose before us on its hill, walls gleaming white in the sun, the Temple rising above all like a crown of gold and marble. The roads thickened with pilgrims—families leading lambs, merchants with their wares, voices lifted in songs of ascent. The smell of dust mixed with woodsmoke and the faint sweetness of blooming almond trees along the way. My heart swelled with the familiar thrill of the feast, but this time it was deeper, sharper, because He was with us—the Lamb of God walking up to the city of the lambs.

Inside the city, the narrow streets echoed with footsteps and bargaining. We moved toward the Temple mount, where the outer court buzzed like a marketplace. Animals lowed and bleated, coins clinked loudly on tables, merchants shouted their prices for doves and cattle. The air was thick with the scent of dung, incense, and sweat. Jesus stopped suddenly amid the chaos. I saw His face change—still calm, but kindled with a holy fire. His eyes flashed as He took cords and fashioned a whip, the leather twisting firmly in His calloused hands.

Then He acted. The whip cracked through the air with sharp authority, tables overturned with heavy crashes that scattered coins across the stone pavement like startled sparrows. Doves fluttered wildly from their cages. “Take these things away!” His voice rang out clear and commanding, echoing off the colonnade walls. “Do not make my Father’s house a house of trade!” Merchants scrambled, their faces twisted in anger and fear, grabbing what they could as animals bolted through the crowd. I stood rooted nearby, my pulse pounding in my ears, the dust rising around my ankles. A holy dread and awe gripped me—my knees felt weak, yet my spirit soared. This was no ordinary man. The zeal of His Father’s house burned in Him like a living flame. I had imagined salvation, when I imagined it at all, as something gentle; now I saw that it began with a refusal to let what was unclean stand in God’s presence. He loved His Father’s house too fiercely to leave it defiled—and I sensed the same love would not be content to leave us defiled either.

Some of the leaders pressed forward, their robes brushing the ground, voices sharp with challenge. “What sign do you show us for doing these things?” Jesus stood tall amid the overturned tables and answered with steady power, “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up.” They scoffed, gesturing at the massive stones around us, but His words sank deep into me, mysterious and weighty. I felt a trembling inside, as if the very ground of my understanding was shifting. Later, much later, I would grasp that He spoke of His body—of a death and a rising that would become the true temple, the real meeting place between God and sinners. In that moment I only knew I had seen glory and authority walk among the courts of God, and that He had laid some cornerstone I would not see finished for a long time.

We remained in Jerusalem for the days of the Passover feast, and the city continued to pulse around us like a living thing. The narrow streets were crowded with pilgrims from every corner of Israel and beyond, their voices rising in a constant murmur of prayer and bargaining. The air carried the mingled scents of roasted lambs, burning incense from the altars, and the sharp tang of animals penned near the Temple. Jesus moved among the people with quiet authority, and I stayed close, my sandals brushing the worn stones that had known the feet of kings and prophets before us.

In those days He performed many signs—miracles that left me breathless. I saw a woman whose hands had been twisted with pain for years reach out to Him; at His gentle word her fingers straightened, supple and strong again. She wept openly, clutching her healed hands to her chest as if afraid they might vanish. Another time, a man blind from birth was led forward by his relatives. Jesus spoke to him with kindness, laid hands on his eyes, and suddenly the man cried out, seeing the bright sky and the faces around him for the first time. His shouts of joy echoed off the Temple walls, drawing a crowd. Each healing stirred a deep trembling in my soul, and slowly I began to see the signs for what they were: not displays of power for their own sake, but small undoings of the ruin sin had worked in the world—previews of what God meant to do for the whole broken race of Adam. Being near Jesus felt like standing close to a blazing fire: it warmed and purified, yet it also exposed every shadow within me. I felt small, yet strangely cherished.

Many began to believe in His name because of these signs, pressing closer in the Temple courts, their faces alight with wonder. Yet I noticed something in Jesus’ eyes—a deep knowing that went beyond our excitement. He did not entrust Himself fully to them, for He knew what was in every human heart. That awareness in Him both comforted and unsettled me; it made me realize He saw not only our hopes but our hidden failings, our fleeting enthusiasms. And still He had come. He knew exactly the kind of people He had set out to save, and He had not turned back. I felt exposed in His presence, yet never rejected, and I began to learn the strange shape of His mercy: He saw the worst of us first, and loved us anyway.

One night, as the city quieted and the oil lamps cast long shadows in the upper rooms where we stayed, a man named Nicodemus came to Jesus under cover of darkness. He was a ruler of the Jews, a Pharisee, his fine robes whispering against the stone floor as he entered. I sat quietly in the corner, watching. The air was still and cool, carrying the faint scent of olive oil from the lamps. Nicodemus spoke with respect, yet I could sense the careful caution in his voice: “Rabbi, we know that you are a teacher come from God, for no one can do these signs that you do unless God is with him.”

Jesus looked at him steadily, the lamp light playing across His face, and answered with words that pierced the quiet like a shaft of light: “Truly, truly, I say to you, unless one is born again he cannot see the kingdom of God.” Nicodemus blinked, confusion crossing his scholarly features. “How can a man be born when he is old? Can he enter a second time into his mother’s womb and be born?” I felt the weight of that question in my own chest—how indeed? Here was a man who had kept the law his whole life, and Jesus told him that all his keeping was not enough, that he needed not improvement but a beginning he could not give himself. The idea seemed impossible, yet coming from Jesus it carried a mysterious pull.

Jesus leaned forward slightly, His voice calm and deep, carrying the authority of one who had seen heaven itself. “Truly, truly, I say to you, unless one is born of water and the Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God. That which is born of the flesh is flesh, and that which is born of the Spirit is spirit. Do not marvel that I said to you, ‘You must be born again.’ The wind blows where it wishes, and you hear its sound, but you do not know where it comes from or where it goes. So it is with everyone who is born of the Spirit.” Salvation, then, was not something a man would achieve but something that would be done to him, as hidden and sovereign as the wind.

I sat motionless, the words sinking into me like rain into dry earth. A strange warmth spread through my limbs, a sense of something vast opening up before me. The night breeze stirred outside, rustling through the narrow street, and I thought of the wind Jesus spoke of—unseen yet powerful, beyond our control. My mind reeled, yet my spirit leaped in recognition. This was no ordinary teaching; it reached into the hidden places of the heart. Nicodemus listened, his face a mixture of awe and struggle, asking more questions as the night deepened. Jesus answered with patience and depth, speaking of the Son of Man lifted up as Moses had lifted the serpent in the wilderness, so that whoever looked to Him in faith might live—and of God so loving the world that He gave His only Son, that whoever believes in Him should not perish but have eternal life. I had thought God’s love was a wage paid to the righteous. Now I heard that it reached down to a perishing world of sinners, and that it would cost the Father His own Son, lifted up like the bronze serpent for everyone bitten by the ancient poison to look upon and be healed.

As the conversation unfolded, I felt my old understanding crumbling further, like clay jars being reshaped by the potter’s hands. Being with Jesus in that quiet upper room was like standing on holy ground; every word He spoke carried life, every glance invited me deeper. A quiet joy mingled with reverent fear in my heart—this man was opening the kingdom to us, not through rituals or bloodlines or careful obedience, but through a new birth and a Son lifted up, a gift only God could give. Nothing in me had purchased it. The night air felt charged, alive with possibility, and I knew, deep in my bones, that this was the best news I had ever heard.

After the long night with Nicodemus, the hours slipping away under the flickering lamps until the sky outside began to pale with dawn, Jesus rose with quiet purpose. We left Jerusalem soon after, heading into the Judean countryside. The road led us out through the city gates, the morning air cool and fresh against our faces, carrying the scent of dew on wildflowers and the distant smoke from village hearth fires. The hills rolled gently before us, terraced with vineyards and dotted with sheep grazing under the watchful eyes of shepherds. Jesus walked with that steady, unhurried gait, His presence like a calm center amid the stirring world. Being with Him on that path made the journey feel sacred, every footfall echoing something deeper than mere travel. My sandals pressed into the soft earth, and I felt the night’s words still burning in my chest like embers that refused to cool—that salvation is a gift, that it comes by a birth from above and a Son given for the world.

We came to a place near the Jordan where there was plenty of water, and there Jesus began to baptize. I stood waist-deep in the cool, flowing river beside Him, the current tugging gently at my legs, the sun warming my shoulders as it climbed higher. The water was clear and refreshing, sparkling as it moved over smooth stones. People came in small groups—humble farmers with calloused hands, women with infants strapped to their backs, even some from the city still marked by the dust of pilgrimage. Jesus would speak to each one with kindness and authority, His voice carrying over the murmur of the river. As they went down into the water and rose again, dripping and renewed, I saw tears on many faces, heard their quiet sobs of release. A holy hush would fall over the scene each time. I felt it too: a cleansing not just of the body but of something reaching into the hidden corners of the soul. This was the new birth made visible—the kingdom breaking in, just as He had said, gentle as water yet powerful enough to remake a life from the inside out.

Not far away, at Aenon near Salim, John the Baptist was still baptizing. The news reached us through travelers: some of John’s own disciples were troubled, coming to him with furrowed brows and questioning voices. “Rabbi,” they said, “the one who was with you across the Jordan, to whom you bore witness—look, He is baptizing, and all are going to Him.” I could imagine John’s response, that fierce yet humble fire in his eyes. He had always pointed away from himself. Later, when the reports came back to us, they carried his words: “A person cannot receive even one thing unless it is given him from heaven. You yourselves bear me witness that I said, ‘I am not the Christ, but I have been sent before Him.’ He who has the bride is the bridegroom. The friend of the bridegroom, who stands and hears him, rejoices greatly at the bridegroom’s voice. Therefore this joy of mine is now complete. He must increase, but I must decrease.” I understood that the whole story was bending toward this one Man—that John, like the prophets before him, had only ever been pointing past himself to the Bridegroom who had finally come for His bride.

Those words reached me like a deep, confirming peace. I pictured John standing by the waters he knew so well, his voice hoarse from preaching, yet radiant with joy at his own decrease. To diminish so that Christ might fill the whole horizon—I sensed that this surrender was not loss but the very pattern of life with Him. The countryside around us seemed brighter, the wildflowers more vivid, the sky a deeper blue, as if all creation leaned in to listen to the Bridegroom’s voice.

But word soon spread to the Pharisees in Jerusalem that Jesus was making and baptizing more disciples than John. I sensed the gathering tension, like storm clouds building on the horizon, though Jesus remained untroubled. In His wisdom, He decided we should leave Judea and return to Galilee. The journey northward was longer this time, the paths winding through Samaria. The sun beat down mercilessly at midday, dust coating our throats and turning our robes pale. We passed fields of waving grain and ancient wells shaded by trees. My feet grew weary, yet walking in step with Him renewed my strength. He spoke little on the road, but His silence was full—comforting, like the steady presence of a father leading through unknown hills. He had set His face toward Samaria on purpose, though I did not yet know it, for there was someone there He meant to find.

We came at last to Sychar in Samaria, weary from the heat. Jesus sat down beside Jacob’s well outside the village while we went into the town to buy food. The well was deep and ancient, its stones cool to the touch, the water far below glistening faintly. The sun was high, the air still and hot. I glanced back at Him as we left—sitting there alone in the shade, dust on His feet, choosing to rest in the one region every devout Jew hurried through. Even then I should have guessed He had come there for a reason. My spirit felt stretched and expectant, alive with the quiet knowledge that following this Man meant stepping continually into mystery and grace.

I returned with the others from the village of Sychar, our arms laden with bread still warm from the ovens, fresh figs, and a skin of wine. The midday heat had begun to ease slightly, but sweat still trickled down my back beneath my robe, and the dust of the road clung to my skin. As we approached Jacob’s well, I saw Jesus still seated there on the low stone rim, His posture relaxed yet attentive. A Samaritan woman stood before Him, her water jar resting on the ground. She was alone—unusual for that hour—and carried herself with a guarded weariness, her veil slightly askew, her eyes cautious, the look of someone accustomed to coming when the other women would not.

I slowed my steps, the others beside me doing the same. We stayed back a respectful distance, close enough to hear but not intrude. The air around the well felt charged, thicker than the ordinary heat, as if heaven itself had drawn near to this dusty patch of earth where a Jewish rabbi was speaking, against every custom, to a Samaritan woman of broken reputation. The woman’s voice carried clearly on the still air: “How is it that you, a Jew, ask for a drink from me, a woman of Samaria?” There was surprise in her tone, mixed with a faint edge of defiance. Jews and Samaritans did not share vessels or pleasant words; the old wound between our peoples ran deep. Yet Jesus crossed that wound as if it were nothing, His voice gentle but piercing, like cool water offered on a scorching day.

“If you knew the gift of God, and who it is that is saying to you, ‘Give me a drink,’ you would have asked Him, and He would have given you living water.” He had come asking a favor, and ended by offering a gift—stooping low to lift her high.

She gestured toward the well, her brow furrowed. “Sir, you have nothing to draw with, and the well is deep. Where do you get that living water? Are you greater than our father Jacob?” Her words held both challenge and curiosity. I felt my own heart quicken, remembering the night with Nicodemus—Jesus speaking of new birth, of unseen realities breaking into the ordinary. Here it was again, unfolding before us in the bright sunlight, only now offered not to a ruler of Israel by night but to a Samaritan woman at noon.

Jesus answered her with patient depth, His eyes steady on hers. “Everyone who drinks of this water will be thirsty again, but whoever drinks of the water that I will give him will never be thirsty forever. The water that I will give him will become in him a spring of water welling up to eternal life.” It was the same gift He had named to Nicodemus—life from within, springing up from God’s own giving—and it was being held out freely to a woman no rabbi I knew would have stopped for.

The woman’s posture shifted. She leaned forward slightly, her voice softening. “Sir, give me this water, so that I will not be thirsty or have to come here to draw.” There was longing beneath her words, a hunger I recognized in my own soul. Then Jesus touched the hidden place in her life: “Go, call your husband, and come here.”

She stiffened. “I have no husband.” Jesus nodded, His voice full of knowing yet free of condemnation. “You are right in saying, ‘I have no husband’; for you have had five husbands, and the one you now have is not your husband. What you have said is true.” He had done with her exactly what He did with everyone—seen straight to the wound she kept covered. But He named her sin not to shame her into leaving; He named it because there is no living water for a thirst we will not admit, and He meant to give her the water.

I watched her face as the truth settled over her. Shock, then a dawning recognition—her eyes widened, color rising in her cheeks. She saw Him truly in that moment. “Sir, I perceive that you are a prophet.” Her voice trembled as she spoke of worship on this mountain or in Jerusalem. Jesus replied with words that seemed to open the sky itself: “Woman, believe me, the hour is coming when neither on this mountain nor in Jerusalem will you worship the Father… God is spirit, and those who worship Him must worship in spirit and truth.” The walls of place and people that men had built around God were coming down; He was opening a way for any heart, anywhere, to come home.

The woman’s response came like a confession and a hope all at once: “I know that Messiah is coming. When He comes, He will tell us all things.” Jesus looked at her with such tenderness and authority that it stirred my own spirit to its depths. “I who speak to you am He.”

My breath caught. A holy awe washed over me, raising the hairs on my arms despite the warmth of the day. This Samaritan woman—outsider, sinner by her own admission—was the first I had ever heard Him tell plainly who He was. Not a ruler of Israel, not a priest in the Temple, but her, at a well, in the heat of the day. I saw then that the plan of salvation was tilted toward exactly the ones the world had written off. She left her jar behind, forgotten, and hurried back toward the village, her steps light and urgent, calling out to the people there.

When she returned leading a crowd, their faces a mixture of skepticism and curiosity, the sun had shifted lower in the sky, casting long golden shadows across the fields. They begged Jesus to stay with them. For two days we remained in Sychar, welcomed into homes where the air smelled of fresh bread and olive oil. Jesus taught in the village square, His voice carrying over the gathered people like a shepherd calling his flock. Many believed because of the woman’s testimony, and even more after hearing Him themselves. “It is no longer because of what you said that we believe,” they told her, “for we have heard for ourselves, and we know that this is indeed the Savior of the world.” The Savior of the world—not of Israel only. I turned the title over in my heart: the Lamb who takes away the sin of the world, the Son given for the world, and now the Savior of the world, confessed first by Samaritans. The circle He had come to gather was wider than I had ever dared to imagine.

I sat among them, listening, feeling the weight of it all settle deeper into my bones. The journey from Jerusalem, the heat of Samaria, the unexpected grace at this well—it all wove together into a tapestry I could scarcely comprehend. Being with Jesus was to watch barriers crumble: Jew and Samaritan, prophet and outcast, the thirsty soul and the Living Water. Each day in His presence stripped away another of my old certainties about who deserved God and who did not, and replaced it with wonder. He had not come to confirm the worthy in their worth; He had come seeking the thirsty, and there was no thirst so disreputable that He would pass it by.

After those two full days in Sychar, where the words of Jesus had taken root in hearts long hardened by division and shame, we departed the village amid a small crowd that followed us to the edge of the fields. The morning air was cool and sweet with the scent of dew on barley stalks, the sun just cresting the hills and painting everything in soft gold. The Samaritan woman walked among the others for a short distance, her face transformed—no longer guarded, but radiant with a quiet joy that made her steps lighter. I felt a deep stirring in my own chest as we left, a sense of expansion, as though my soul had been enlarged by watching grace cross every barrier of race and reputation. Jesus had given living water not only to her, but somehow to all of us who watched—and I began to understand that this was the very thing He had come to do.

The road north into Galilee stretched before us, climbing gradually through Samaria’s valleys before descending again. The journey took us through rugged terrain where ancient olive trees twisted like prophets in prayer, their leaves shimmering silver in the breeze. Dust rose around our ankles with each step, and the midday heat pressed down heavily, yet walking beside Jesus made the miles bearable. His presence was like a steady anchor—unhurried, strong, radiating a peace that seemed to quiet even the weariness in my legs and the questions in my mind. I watched Him as He walked, the simple fold of His robe against His shoulder, the calm set of His jaw. As we went He preached a single blazing word wherever the people gathered—“The time is fulfilled, and the kingdom of God is at hand; repent and believe in the gospel”—and I began to hear that call not as a demand to earn the kingdom but as an open hand inviting empty ones to receive it. Being near Him filled me with both reverence and comfort, as if I were a child following a father through unknown country. My heart felt full, yet hungry for more.

We crossed back into Galilee, and the people there received Him gladly. Word had spread from the Passover in Jerusalem—of the signs He had done, the Temple cleansed, the sick healed. Villages we passed through buzzed with quiet excitement; men paused their plowing, women at the wells turned to watch us. The air carried the familiar smells of home—freshly turned soil, woodsmoke from cooking fires, the faint salt of the distant lake. I felt a swell of awe at how the news of Him had traveled ahead like heralds, and a deeper wonder still that the One they were running to greet had come to do for them what they could not have dreamed to ask.

We came at length to Nazareth, the town where Jesus had grown from boy to man. The streets were narrow and familiar to Him, the smell of sawdust and warm bread drifting from the houses, the hills rising brown and quiet around the little valley. Word had gone before us of all He had done in Capernaum, and the people watched Him with a mixture of pride and wariness, the way one watches a son who has gone away and come home changed.

On the Sabbath we went into the synagogue, as was His custom. The room was close and warm, the murmur of greetings fading as He stood to read. The attendant handed Him the scroll of the prophet Isaiah, and I watched His hands unroll it with care, searching out the place. The whole assembly grew still. His voice filled the small room, steady and clear: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because He has anointed me to proclaim good news to the poor. He has sent me to proclaim liberty to the captives and recovering of sight to the blind, to set at liberty those who are oppressed, to proclaim the year of the Lord’s favor.” Here, in His own chosen words, was the shape of His mission: not to the strong but to the poor, the captive, the blind, the oppressed—to people who had nothing to bring but their need.

He rolled up the scroll, gave it back to the attendant, and sat down. Every eye was fixed on Him. Into that waiting silence He said, “Today this Scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing.” I felt the words settle over the room like the hush before dawn, every face turned toward Him, waiting. The long-promised year of favor had not come on some distant horizon; it had walked into their synagogue and sat down.

At first they marveled at the gracious words that came from His mouth. But the wonder soured even as I watched it. “Is not this Joseph’s son?” someone said, low, and others took it up, their faces beginning to harden. They had known Him as the carpenter’s boy; they could not bear that He should speak as one sent from God. Jesus answered their unspoken demand without flinching: “Doubtless you will quote to me this proverb, ‘Physician, heal yourself.’ What we have heard you did at Capernaum, do here also in your hometown.” Then He spoke of Elijah, sent in the famine not to the widows of Israel but to a widow of Sidon, and of Elisha, who cleansed no leper in Israel but Naaman the Syrian. He was telling them the very thing I had been slowly learning at the well: that God’s saving mercy spills past the borders of the deserving and reaches the outsider who will receive it over the insider who will not.

The room turned like a tide. I felt the heat rise before I fully grasped the words—shoulders squaring, voices climbing, hands reaching. They rose up together and drove Him out of the town, pressing and shoving Him toward the brow of the hill on which Nazareth was built, meaning to throw Him down headlong. My heart hammered against my ribs; I could not reach Him through the crush of bodies. And then—I cannot fully account for what I saw—He passed through the midst of them and went on His way. The hands that had grasped at Him closed on nothing. Their fury broke against Him like water against a stone and ran off into the dust.

I followed Him down the road, my breath ragged, my thoughts reeling. The very words that had stirred my own heart had kindled something near to murder in theirs. I began to understand that the light He carried did not only warm; it divided. The grace that was good news to the poor was an offense to those who were sure they had no need of it. To welcome Him was life. To insist on one’s own sufficiency was to be left standing on the edge of a hill with empty hands, not knowing how He had slipped away.

We came again to Cana, the very place where water had first become wine. The village looked the same—stone houses clustered together, children playing in the narrow lanes, the scent of baking bread drifting from open doors. But everything felt different now, charged with memory. A certain nobleman from Capernaum, an official in Herod’s service, sought Jesus out. His face was drawn with desperation, eyes hollow from sleepless nights. He approached with urgent steps, his fine cloak dusty from the hard ride, and begged Him, “Sir, come down to Capernaum, for my son is at the point of death.”

I stood close enough to see the tremor in the man’s hands as he spoke. His voice cracked with fatherly fear—the kind that strips away all pride. Jesus looked at him, and at the small crowd gathering, and said with measured authority, “Unless you see signs and wonders you will not believe.” The words hung heavy in the warm air. The nobleman’s face tightened, but he pressed on, almost pleading, “Sir, come down before my child dies.”

Then Jesus spoke words that pierced the moment like sunlight breaking through clouds: “Go; your son will live.” The nobleman’s eyes met Jesus’, and in that instant I saw belief take hold—raw, desperate trust. He did not argue or demand proof. He simply turned and began the journey back to Capernaum, his steps hurried yet steadier, as if carrying a fragile hope. He had nothing to lean on but the bare word of Jesus, and on that word he set out for home.

The next day, as we remained in Cana, servants from the nobleman’s household found us. Their faces shone with astonishment. They told us the boy had begun to recover at the exact hour Jesus had spoken the word—the fever breaking suddenly, strength returning to his small limbs as if life itself had been commanded to return. The father had asked them the hour, and when they told him, he knew. He and his entire household believed.

I stood there in the village square, the sun warm on my face, my heart pounding with the same awe I had felt at the wedding. Another sign. Not with jars and wine this time, but across distance, through a father’s faith. I felt tears prick at my eyes unbidden, a trembling deep in my spirit. This Man spoke, and death itself yielded. And I saw something in that father I knew I would need: he had been saved his son not by anything he could see or do, but by taking Jesus at His word and walking home on it. That, I began to understand, was the whole posture of faith—to receive the promise and stake everything on the One who made it. The road behind us and the road ahead seemed bathed in the same light—His light—and I followed, more certain with every step that I had left everything for the only thing worth having.

After the nobleman and his servants departed with joy lighting their faces, we did not linger long in Cana. Jesus led us down toward the Sea of Galilee once more, the road descending gently through terraced hills where vines heavy with young grapes clung to the slopes. The afternoon sun warmed our backs, and the air carried the sweet scent of ripening fruit mixed with the faint, salty promise of the lake ahead. My feet knew this path by now, yet each journey with Him felt fresh, as though the land itself responded to His presence. Dust rose softly with our steps, and I walked close behind Him, watching the steady rhythm of His shoulders. A deep contentment settled in me, mingled with expectancy. Every mile seemed to whisper that greater things were unfolding.

We reached the shore near Capernaum as the sun dipped lower, painting the water in hues of gold and deepening blue. Fishing boats bobbed gently at the water’s edge, their wooden hulls creaking softly against the pebbles. The smell of the lake—fresh water, fish, and wet nets—filled my nostrils, familiar and comforting. Several of us had been fishermen before following Him; the sight stirred old memories in my chest. Jesus stopped near the water, the gentle waves lapping at His feet, and the crowds soon found Him. They pressed in eagerly, hungry for His teaching, their voices a low murmur of hope and need.

Simon Peter was there with his brother Andrew, along with James and his brother John, the sons of Zebedee. They had returned to their boats after a long, fruitless night on the water. I saw the weariness in their faces as they washed their nets—broad shoulders slumped, hands raw from the ropes. Jesus stepped into Simon’s boat and asked him to push out a little from the land. From there, seated in the boat with the water rocking gently beneath Him, He taught the crowds on the shore. His voice carried clearly over the water, rich and full of authority, speaking of the kingdom as a treasure hidden in a field, as a net cast into the sea. I stood on the shore among the people, my heart swelling within me. The words sank deep, nourishing places I had not known were empty. Being near Him while He taught was like standing under a steady rain after drought—reviving, cleansing.

When He finished, He turned to Simon. “Put out into the deep and let down your nets for a catch.” Simon hesitated, his voice rough with exhaustion. “Master, we toiled all night and took nothing! But at your word I will let down the nets.” I watched as they rowed out, the oars dipping rhythmically into the sparkling water. The sun was lower now, casting long reflections across the lake. Then it happened. The nets went down, and suddenly the water churned. Fish—hundreds upon hundreds—filled the nets so quickly and so abundantly that the cords strained and the boats began to sink under the weight. Shouts rose from the boats—astonishment, laughter mixed with alarm. Simon and the others waved frantically for help from the other boat. James and John rowed over swiftly, their faces alive with wonder as they hauled in the overflowing catch together. The boats rode low in the water, silver fish flashing and slapping against the wood, their scales catching the dying light like living jewels.

I waded out to help, the cool lake water rising around my knees, my hands plunging into the heaving nets. The fish were heavy, thrashing with life, their wet bodies cool and slippery. My arms ached from the effort, yet my spirit soared. Simon fell to his knees right there in the boat, right in the midst of the miracle, water sloshing around him. His voice broke as he looked at Jesus: “Depart from me, for I am a sinful man, O Lord!” The raw confession pierced me. I felt it too—a holy fear rising in my chest, my own unworthiness laid bare before such power and kindness. And here I saw something I would see again and again until I finally understood it: the sinner’s instinct is to flee from holiness, but Jesus’ answer is to draw the sinner near. He looked at Simon with eyes full of compassion and said, “Do not be afraid; from now on you will be catching men.” He did not wait for Simon to make himself worthy; He laid hold of an unworthy man and gave him a calling.

That moment on the water changed everything. We brought the boats to land, the abundant catch still shimmering in the hulls, and they left it all—the nets, the boats, the fish, their old lives. Simon, Andrew, James, and John followed Him that day with a wholehearted surrender I felt echoing in my own soul. Being with Jesus meant watching the ordinary burst open into the extraordinary: empty nets filled, weary men transformed into fishers of men. I felt my old world slipping further away, like sand through open fingers, replaced by something vast and eternal. The lakeshore that evening, with its gentle waves and the scent of fish and salt, became holy ground beneath our feet. I walked behind Him as the stars began to appear overhead, my spirit quiet yet alive, understanding a little more that grace does not find us fit—it lays hold of us as we are and makes us follow.

We made our way into Capernaum that same evening, the miraculous catch of fish still fresh on our hands and in our minds. The town nestled close to the shore, its dark basalt stone houses glowing softly in the fading light, the air thick with the smells of cooking fires, baked bread, and the ever-present tang of the lake. My clothes were damp from the water, my arms weary from hauling nets, yet a fire burned steadily in my chest—an excitement laced with holy fear that refused to let me rest.

On the Sabbath, we went together into the synagogue. The building was modest but filled with reverence: stone walls cool to the touch, the scent of worn scrolls and olive oil lamps heavy in the air. Men sat on the floor or low benches, their prayer shawls draped over their shoulders, murmuring familiar blessings. Jesus stood to teach, and from the first word, silence fell like a blanket. His voice was clear and full of authority, not like the scribes who quoted endlessly without power. He spoke of the kingdom as if He had walked its streets Himself. I sat near the back, my heart pounding in rhythm with His words, feeling them sink into me like good seed into fertile soil. This was no ordinary rabbi. The air itself seemed to tremble with the weight of what He said.

Suddenly, a man cried out from the midst of the congregation—a tortured, unnatural shriek that tore through the holy quiet. He convulsed, eyes wild, foam at the corners of his mouth. “What have you to do with us, Jesus of Nazareth?” the voice snarled through him, harsh and demonic. “Have you come to destroy us? I know who you are—the Holy One of God!” The sound of it sent a chill racing down my spine; I felt the hairs on my arms rise. The man’s body jerked violently as the unclean spirit fought within him.

Jesus turned toward him without fear, His face calm yet commanding. “Be silent,” He said firmly, “and come out of him!” The man convulsed once more, a loud cry echoing off the stone walls, and then the spirit left him. The man collapsed, then rose, blinking in confusion but whole—his eyes clear, his body at peace. Whispers rippled through the synagogue, growing into astonished murmurs. “What is this?” people asked one another. “A new teaching with authority! He commands even the unclean spirits, and they obey Him!” I sat motionless, my breath shallow, a deep awe pressing on my chest like a physical weight. I had imagined our bondage as a matter of bad habits and broken laws; now I saw there was a darker captivity beneath it, real powers that held men in chains—and that this Man had walked into the world to break them. To save sinners was not only to forgive them but to wrench them out of the grip of the enemy who claimed them. The demons knew who He was when men did not, and they trembled, for His coming was their undoing.

We left the synagogue and went straight to the house of Simon and Andrew. The modest home smelled of fresh fish and herbs, the midday sun streaming through the open doorway. Simon’s mother-in-law lay in the inner room, burning with a severe fever. Her face was flushed and drawn with pain, her breathing labored. Jesus went to her bedside without hesitation. He took her hand gently in His own—those strong, carpenter’s hands—and lifted her up. At once the fever left her. Color returned to her cheeks in a healthy glow. She stood, fully restored, and immediately began serving us, moving about the house with renewed strength, preparing food as if she had never been ill. I watched in silent wonder, my throat tight with emotion. One touch from Him, and sickness fled like shadows before the dawn—and the very strength He gave her, she poured straight back out in service to Him. It struck me as the whole movement of salvation in small: He lays hold of us where we lie helpless, raises us by His own power, and the raising itself frees us to serve the One who gave us back our life.

As evening came and the sun dipped below the hills, painting the lake in fiery oranges and purples, the whole city gathered at the door. The news had spread like wind over the water. People brought the sick and those oppressed by demons—men, women, and children crowding the narrow street, their faces etched with desperation and hope. The air filled with the sounds of weeping, pleading voices, and the shuffling of many feet. Torches flickered, casting dancing shadows on the walls. Jesus went out among them, laying His hands on each one. I moved through the crowd helping calm the people and keep order. One by one, after a touch from Jesus, they were healed. Demons cried out as they fled, their shrieks cutting through the night before falling silent. The healed ones laughed and wept for joy, embracing their families. I felt overwhelmed by the sheer abundance of mercy pouring out through Him. He turned no one away for being too broken or too unclean; He rationed nothing. Being with Jesus in that moment was like watching the very heart of God beating for His people—compassion flowing freely, powerfully, without limit, the way I was beginning to believe He would one day pour out salvation itself.

That night, long after the crowds had gone and the town quieted under a canopy of stars, I lay on the roof of the house, the cool night breeze brushing my face. The events of the day replayed in my mind: the synagogue, the demon, the fever leaving a woman’s body, the sea of faces made whole. A profound sense of privilege filled me, mixed with the growing awareness of how much I still did not understand. Yet I knew this with certainty—I would follow this Man anywhere. In His presence, the broken world seemed to be mending, one touch, one word at a time, as though the long ruin were being quietly rolled back.

The night was deep and still when I finally drifted into sleep on the rooftop, the stars wheeling slowly overhead like silent witnesses. The cool breeze from the lake carried the faint rhythm of lapping waves, and my body ached from the long day, yet my spirit remained strangely alert, as if it refused to fully rest in the afterglow of all we had seen.

Before the sky had fully lightened, while the town still slept and the first faint gray of dawn touched the eastern hills, I stirred at the sound of movement below. Jesus had risen. I watched from the edge of the roof as He slipped quietly out of the house, His figure a shadow against the dim light, heading alone toward the desolate places outside Capernaum. The hills were rocky and barren there, dotted with scrub and wild olive trees. I did not follow immediately, sensing this was His sacred time with the Father. But later, when Simon and the others woke and found Him gone, we went searching. The morning air was crisp and cool against my skin, dew still clinging to the sparse grass underfoot. My sandals grew damp as we climbed the rocky path, hearts pounding not just from the effort but from a growing hunger to be near Him again.

We found Him in a quiet hollow among the hills, kneeling in prayer. The first rays of sun were breaking over the ridge, bathing Him in soft golden light. He rose when He saw us, dust on the knees of His robe, His face peaceful yet purposeful. Simon, breathless, spoke for all of us: “Everyone is looking for you!” The urgency in his voice was plain—the crowds from last night were already stirring back in the town, hungry for more. But Jesus looked out over the lake shimmering in the distance and said calmly, “Let us go on to the next towns, that I may preach there also. For that is why I came out.” His words carried a quiet resolve that settled something deep inside me. He would not be held even by a town full of grateful people, because the good news had to run to as many as would receive it, and He meant to carry it to them all.

We traveled from village to village throughout Galilee in the days that followed. The roads wound through fertile valleys and over gentle hills, the air sweet with the scent of blooming wildflowers and ripening grain. Dust rose around our feet in soft clouds, and the sun warmed our shoulders as we walked. Jesus preached in their synagogues—simple gatherings of farmers, fishermen, and craftsmen who listened with rapt attention. His teaching was like nothing I had ever heard: full of life and fire, yet tender as a shepherd with a lamb. He spoke of the kingdom of God as if it were a seed planted now, growing secretly yet powerfully among us. I walked behind Him, feeling the weight of each word settle into my bones. My old ways of thinking—narrow, bound by tradition and fear—felt as though they were loosening, cracking open like dry earth after rain.

One afternoon we came to a leper who approached us on the outskirts of a village. The man was a pitiful sight: his skin ravaged by the disease, white patches and open sores visible where his ragged clothes did not cover him. He kept his distance as the law required, yet fell to his knees in the dust, his voice breaking with desperate hope. “Lord, if you will, you can make me clean.” The air around us seemed to still. I felt a surge of pity and awe—pity for the man’s suffering, awe at his raw faith. Jesus did not draw back. Instead, He reached out with compassion shining in His eyes and touched him—actually touched the unclean flesh. “I will,” He said gently, “be clean.” At once the leprosy left the man. His skin became whole and smooth right before our eyes, like a dead branch suddenly bursting with green life. The man wept openly, trembling as he touched his restored face and arms. Jesus instructed him quietly to show himself to the priest and offer the gift Moses commanded, but the news spread quickly anyway. My heart hammered in my chest as I witnessed it. Under the law the unclean defiled the clean, and no one reached across that line; yet Jesus crossed it without flinching, and instead of catching the man’s defilement, He gave the man His own cleanness. I began to see how He would save us—not by keeping a safe distance from our uncleanness, but by laying His hand on it and taking it into Himself, so that what touched Him came away clean.

The crowds grew wherever we went, pressing in with their needs, yet Jesus often withdrew again to lonely places to pray. I began to understand that His power flowed from that hidden communion with the Father. Following Him was teaching me to listen, to watch, to wait. Each day brought new wonders, new teachings that sank deeper into my soul, and a growing certainty that I was walking in the company of the One Israel had waited for through long centuries of darkness. My spirit felt both hushed and exhilarated, like a sail filled with a strong, steady wind carrying me toward an unseen shore.

After the healing of the leper, word of Jesus spread like wildfire through the hills and villages of Galilee. We returned to Capernaum, the familiar path now feeling almost like home despite how much had changed within me. The lake glittered under the midday sun as we approached, its surface rippling gently in the breeze, carrying the ever-present smells of fish and salt water. My robe was dusty from the road, my feet sore, but a quiet strength seemed to flow from simply walking near Him. Jesus moved with purpose yet without haste, His presence like a deep river—calm on the surface, yet carrying immense power beneath.

We entered the town, and the crowds quickly found us again. They pressed around the house where we stayed, filling the narrow street until there was no room even at the door. The air grew thick with the scent of many bodies, dust, and expectation. Jesus was teaching inside, His voice steady and full of life, when four men arrived carrying their paralyzed friend on a mat. The poor man lay motionless, his limbs thin and useless, his eyes filled with a quiet desperation that pierced my heart. His friends, faces streaked with sweat and determination, could not push through the crowd. So they climbed the outer stairs to the roof, their sandals scraping against the clay tiles. I stepped outside and looked up, shielding my eyes from the sun, as they began tearing away the thatch and beams with urgent hands. Dirt and pieces of roofing fell into the room below in small showers. The people inside murmured in surprise, but Jesus simply looked up with calm authority.

The mat was lowered carefully through the opening, ropes creaking, until the paralyzed man lay directly before Jesus on the floor. Dust still drifted down around him like a veil. I watched from the doorway, my chest tight with anticipation and pity. Jesus looked at the man, then at his friends whose faith had torn through every obstacle, and said words that silenced the room: “Son, your sins are forgiven.” The man had been carried there for his legs, and Jesus spoke first to his sins, as though the deeper paralysis—the one beneath the visible one—was the guilt that bound him to death. A ripple of shock went through the scribes sitting there—teachers of the law with stern faces and crossed arms. I could see the offense in their eyes as they thought to themselves, “Why does this man speak like this? He is blaspheming! Who can forgive sins but God alone?”

Jesus knew their thoughts. He turned to them, His gaze steady and piercing, and asked, “Why do you question these things in your hearts? Which is easier, to say to the paralytic, ‘Your sins are forgiven,’ or to say, ‘Rise, take up your bed and walk’? But that you may know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins—” He looked back at the man on the mat, His voice ringing with power—“I say to you, rise, pick up your bed, and go home.”

The moment that followed is burned into my memory. The man’s eyes widened. Strength flowed visibly into his wasted limbs. He stirred, then sat up. A gasp rose from everyone watching. Slowly, deliberately, he swung his legs over the edge of the mat, planted his feet on the floor, and stood. His face broke into a smile of pure astonishment and joy. He rolled up his mat, tucked it under his arm, and walked out through the crowd, praising God with a loud voice. The people parted before him, stunned into silence at first, then erupting in awe. “We never saw anything like this!” they cried. “Glory to God!”

My knees felt weak as I watched him go. Tears stung my eyes unbidden. I had seen water turned to wine, demons cast out, lepers cleansed—but this was different. Forgiveness and healing had flowed together from the same source, and at last I understood what I had only half-seen before. He had not come merely to mend bodies; the healings were signs, pointing to the greater thing—that the Son of Man had authority on earth to forgive sins. This was the heart of why He had come. My own sins, hidden though they were, seemed exposed in the light of His authority, yet instead of shame I felt hope—deep, cleansing hope. In that dusty room, with sunlight slanting through the broken roof, I saw that my deepest need was not for my circumstances to be mended but for my guilt to be lifted, and that here, in flesh and blood, stood the One with authority to lift it.

We continued ministering in Capernaum and the surrounding region in the days that followed. The crowds never seemed to thin. Jesus moved among them with tireless compassion, yet He still slipped away at times to pray in the lonely places before dawn. I began to treasure those quiet mornings when I could watch Him return, His face refreshed as if He had drunk from a hidden spring. Each day with Him peeled away another layer of my old self, leaving me more awake, more alive, more hungry for the kingdom He carried within Him like a priceless treasure.

After the paralytic rose and walked out carrying his mat, the atmosphere in Capernaum remained charged for days. People talked of nothing else. Jesus continued teaching in homes and open places, and I stayed near Him, listening closely to every word. One afternoon, as we passed the tax booth by the lakeshore, Jesus stopped. The collector there was Levi, son of Alphaeus—a man most of us avoided because of his work for the Romans. He sat surrounded by coins and records, his face set in the careful mask of someone used to suspicion.

Jesus looked directly at him and said simply, “Follow me.” Levi stood at once. He left the booth, the money, the ledgers—everything—just as he was. I saw the surprise in his eyes turn quickly to resolve. That same evening, Levi hosted a meal in his house. Many other tax collectors and people known for loose living came. They filled the rooms, eating and talking together around the low tables. I sat among them, watching Jesus recline at the table as if He belonged there, speaking with them naturally and without any sign of discomfort.

The Pharisees noticed. Some of their scribes stood outside, murmuring loudly enough for us to hear: “Why does He eat with tax collectors and sinners?” Their tone was sharp with disapproval. Jesus heard them and answered clearly, “Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick. I came not to call the righteous, but sinners.” His words hung in the air, steady and kind, and they gathered up everything I had been slowly learning into a single sentence. The well had no need of Him; the sick did. He had not come for the people who imagined themselves righteous, but for the ones who knew they were sick unto death. I had once thought of myself as better than men like Levi—and in that very thought I had nearly disqualified myself from the mercy I needed most. The kingdom reached exactly the places we counted unworthy, because those were the only places that knew they were ill. It humbled me deeply and made me grateful, for the first time, to know my own sickness.

Not long after, some people came asking why Jesus’ disciples did not fast as the disciples of John and the Pharisees did. Jesus replied, “Can the wedding guests fast while the bridegroom is with them? As long as they have the bridegroom with them, they cannot fast. The days will come when the bridegroom is taken away from them, and then they will fast in that day.” He continued with images of new cloth and old garments, new wine and old wineskins—warning that His way could not be forced into the old patterns without tearing everything apart. I listened carefully, sensing that what He brought could not simply be stitched onto the old religion of earning and deserving; it was a new thing, and it would burst the old wineskins wide open. The Bridegroom had come to His feast, and the only fitting answer to His presence was joy. His words made even the coming sorrow He hinted at—the day the bridegroom would be taken away—feel like part of some larger mercy I could not yet trace.

When a feast of the Jews drew near, we went up again to Jerusalem. The city was crowded as before, the streets thick with pilgrims, the smoke of the altar rising into a pale sky. But Jesus led us first to a place I had not seen—a pool near the Sheep Gate, called in our tongue Bethesda, ringed by five covered colonnades. Beneath those roofs lay a multitude of the sick: the blind, the lame, the withered, stretched out on mats in the shade, waiting. The air hung heavy with the smell of sickness and the low sound of suffering, and something in my chest tightened to see so much hopelessness gathered into one place. I would have hurried past it; He walked straight in, as if such a place were exactly what He had come for.

One man among them had been an invalid for thirty-eight years—longer than I had been alive. He lay where perhaps he had lain for much of that time, his body wasted, his eyes gone dull with the long habit of disappointment. Jesus stopped before him. “Do you want to be healed?” He asked. The man did not answer Yes; he answered out of his weariness: “Sir, I have no one to put me into the pool when the water is stirred, and while I am going another steps down before me.” He had no one, and no strength to save himself—and that, I was beginning to see, was precisely the condition Jesus came to meet. He did not wait for the man to drag himself to the water. Jesus looked at him with that steady gaze I had come to know, and said, “Rise, take up your bed and walk.” At once—at once—the strength I had watched pour into others poured into him. He rose, rolled up the mat that had been his prison, and walked. I stood gaping as he passed me, carrying the bed that for so long had carried him.

But it was the Sabbath. The leaders saw the man with his mat and rebuked him rather than rejoice with him: “It is not lawful for you to take up your bed.” When they learned who had healed him, their anger turned toward Jesus. The wariness I had first felt among the Pharisees by the Jordan hardened now into open hostility, plain on their faces in the bright Temple light. It unsettled me that the same act could draw a helpless man to his feet and harden the hearts of the watching—as if the mercy itself were sorting us.

Jesus did not retreat from it. He answered them with words that lifted the veil higher than I was ready for: “My Father is working until now, and I am working.” I heard the breath go out of the men around me. To call God His own Father, making Himself equal with God—this they could not abide. Yet He pressed on, and I drank in every word though I could scarcely hold it: that the Son does only what He sees the Father doing; that as the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so also the Son gives life to whom He will; that an hour was coming, and now was, when the dead would hear the voice of the Son of God and those who heard would live. He had just raised a man from thirty-eight years of living death, and now He claimed that the same voice would one day call the truly dead out of their graves. The healing at the pool was only a small picture of the life He had come to give.

When they demanded proof, He spoke of witnesses. John the Baptist had borne witness to the truth, He said—a burning and shining lamp in whose light they had been willing, for a while, to rejoice. The very works He was doing bore witness that the Father had sent Him. The Father Himself bore witness. And the Scriptures they searched so carefully, supposing that in them they had life, were themselves pointing to Him—yet they would not come to Him to have that life. “Moses wrote of me,” He said. “But if you do not believe his writings, how will you believe my words?” It struck me that a man could know every letter of the law and still miss the Life the law was pointing to; the Scriptures were a road, and He was the home at the end of it.

I walked out from under the colonnades into the open courts with my thoughts turning over and over. I had watched a man stand upright after thirty-eight years on his back, and I had heard the One who raised him claim the right to raise the dead and to judge the living. The leaders had heard the same things and reached only for stones. I understood, dimly, that I was being asked to settle what they would not: whether the voice that had called a cripple to his feet was the same voice that would one day call me, and all the dead, up out of the dust. And if it was, then life itself was a gift held out in His hand, to be received and not earned.

One Sabbath we were walking through the fields. The disciples picked heads of grain as we went, rubbing them in our hands to eat. Some Pharisees challenged Him immediately: “Look, why are they doing what is not lawful on the Sabbath?” Jesus answered them by reminding them of David eating the bread of the Presence and of the Sabbath being made for man, not man for the Sabbath. Then He declared, “The Son of Man is lord even of the Sabbath.” I turned it over as we walked: the day of rest had been given as a gift to weary people, not laid on them as another burden—and the One walking beside us was Lord of it, the true rest these fields and feasts had only ever pointed toward.

Another Sabbath, in the synagogue, a man with a withered hand was present. The religious leaders watched Jesus closely to see if He would heal on the Sabbath. Jesus called the man forward and asked the critics plainly, “Is it lawful on the Sabbath to do good or to do harm, to save life or to kill?” They remained silent. He looked around at them with sorrow and anger at their hardness, then said to the man, “Stretch out your hand.” The man did, and it was restored, whole and strong like the other. The leaders went out at once and began plotting against Him. I felt the tension rising, yet Jesus remained calm and purposeful. It sobered me to see that the very mercy that restored a withered hand was driving His enemies toward His death—that even now His saving work and the cross it would cost Him were quietly bound together. It stirred a quiet resolve in me to stay close, no matter what might come.

After the growing tension in the synagogue, Jesus withdrew with us toward the sea. Many followed from Galilee, Judea, Jerusalem, Idumea, and even from beyond the Jordan and the regions around Tyre and Sidon. The crowds were large, pressing in to touch Him because power went out from Him and healed them all. I stayed near, watching as people with various afflictions came forward—some carried on mats, others limping or led by the hand. Jesus received each one with steady attention. I saw relief wash over their faces as diseases left them and unclean spirits departed with cries. His calm authority never wavered. The mercy seemed inexhaustible, flowing out to whoever would press near and reach for Him, and I felt a deep sense of privilege mixed with responsibility, as though I were witnessing something sacred that demanded my full attention and loyalty.

One day He went up on the mountain and called certain ones of us to Himself. I climbed with the others, the path steady beneath my feet. When we reached a level place, He stopped and looked at each of us in turn. His gaze was knowing and purposeful. From the larger group of disciples, He chose twelve whom He named apostles, that they might be with Him and that He might send them out to preach. Simon, whom He called Peter, and Andrew his brother. James and John, the sons of Zebedee, whom He named Boanerges, that is, sons of thunder. Then Philip, Bartholomew, Matthew (who had been Levi the tax collector), Thomas, James the son of Alphaeus, Thaddaeus, Simon the Zealot, and Judas Iscariot, who would later betray Him.

I was among those called close in this way. When Jesus looked at me and included me in that number, I felt a quiet weight settle on my shoulders—not burdensome, but real. He had not chosen us for what we brought; He chose us first to be with Him, and only then to be sent, as if the being-with had to come before any work could flow from it. It was as if He was entrusting me with something far beyond my own ability. I felt both small and strengthened in His presence, aware of my shortcomings yet drawn forward by His grace. And the name He spoke last—Judas, who would betray Him—lodged in me like a splinter, a sober reminder that being near Him was not the same as being saved by Him; even the closeness was a gift to be received, not a possession to be presumed upon.

He began to teach the larger crowd that had gathered on the level ground. His words came with gentle authority: “Blessed are you who are poor, for yours is the kingdom of God. Blessed are you who are hungry now, for you shall be satisfied. Blessed are you who weep now, for you shall laugh.” He spoke of love for enemies, of not judging others, of good fruit coming from a good heart. “Why do you call me ‘Lord, Lord,’ and not do what I tell you?” He asked at one point. The teaching was direct, practical, and searching. I felt it examining my own life, exposing where my thoughts and actions fell short. Yet there was mercy in the challenge. He pronounced His blessing not on the strong and full but on the poor, the hungry, the weeping—on people who had nothing in their hands and knew it. The righteousness He described was so far beyond me that it drove me, not to despair, but to lean harder on Him; I saw that the same lips that set the impossible standard were the lips that had been forgiving sinners all along. Sitting there among the apostles and the people, I found myself wanting to follow more closely, even as I recognized how much I still needed Him to change.

After He finished teaching, we descended with Him. A centurion’s servant was ill and near death. The centurion, a man of authority, sent elders to ask Jesus to come and heal his servant. When Jesus drew near the house, the centurion sent friends with a message: “Lord, do not trouble yourself, for I am not worthy to have you come under my roof. Therefore I did not presume to come to you. But say the word, and let my servant be healed.” I stood nearby and saw the respect and faith in the man’s approach, even through messengers. Jesus marveled at him and said to the crowd, “I tell you, not even in Israel have I found such faith.” When the messengers returned, they found the servant well. A Gentile soldier, an outsider to the covenant, had grasped what many in Israel had not—that Jesus needed only to speak and it was done—and his faith in the bare word was counted greater than all the privilege of birth.

These events deepened my conviction. Each act of mercy, each teaching, each quiet look from Jesus confirmed that I was exactly where I needed to be. Being with Him was reshaping my understanding of God’s kingdom—a kingdom that welcomed the outsider, counted faith above status, and called ordinary men like me by sheer grace into extraordinary purpose. I was beginning to see that the only thing He ever asked of the people He saved was that they trust Him, and that even this trust seemed to be something He drew out of them rather than something they manufactured.

We continued traveling through the towns and villages of Galilee. One day we approached Nain, a small town not far from Capernaum. As we drew near the gate, a funeral procession came out toward us. The air was heavy with sorrow. A young man had died, the only son of a widow. She walked behind the bier, her face etched with grief so deep it seemed to hollow her out. The mourners followed, their laments low and steady. I felt the weight of her loss settle in my own chest—a mother burying her child, now utterly alone in the world.

Jesus stopped. His eyes rested on the widow with compassion so clear and strong it seemed to fill the space between them. No one had asked Him; her need alone moved Him. He spoke to her gently, “Do not weep.” Then He stepped forward and touched the bier. The bearers stood still. In a voice calm and full of authority He said, “Young man, I say to you, arise.” The young man sat up at once and began to speak. The procession turned to stunned silence, then to joy and fear. The widow embraced her son, weeping now with relief and wonder. Those around us glorified God, saying, “A great prophet has arisen among us!” and “God has visited His people!” I stood there, heart pounding, unable to look away. The power in Jesus’ word had reached into death itself and pulled life back. Their cry stayed with me—God has visited His people—for I was beginning to grasp that this was the heart of it: God had not stayed far off, content to pity us from heaven, but had come down into our funerals to undo death from the inside. If He could speak life into a corpse, then the salvation He carried went all the way down to the grave, and even there it would not be stopped.

Later, messengers came from John the Baptist, who was now in prison. They asked Jesus directly, “Are you the one who is to come, or shall we look for another?” John’s doubt, even from prison, touched me. Jesus answered them by pointing to what they could see: the blind receiving sight, the lame walking, lepers cleansed, the deaf hearing, the dead raised, the poor having good news preached to them. Then He spoke of John with honor, calling him more than a prophet, the messenger who prepared the way. I listened carefully, feeling the tension between expectation and reality. Being with Jesus meant learning that the kingdom came not always in the dramatic deliverance we imagined—not yet the breaking of every prison—but in these quiet, unstoppable acts of mercy that were themselves the proof of who He was.

One evening, a Pharisee named Simon invited Jesus to dinner at his house. We went, and I sat at the edge of the room, observing. A woman from the city, known for her sinful life, entered while we were reclining at the table. She carried an alabaster flask of ointment. She stood behind Jesus at His feet, weeping. Her tears fell on His feet, and she wiped them with her hair, then kissed them and anointed them with the ointment. The fragrance filled the room—rich and sweet. Simon thought to himself that if Jesus were a prophet, He would know what kind of woman this was and reject her. But Jesus turned to him and told a parable about two debtors, one owing much and one little, both forgiven. “Which will love the creditor more?” He asked. Simon answered correctly, the one forgiven more. Jesus then looked at the woman and said to Simon, “Her sins, which are many, are forgiven, for she loved much. But he who is forgiven little, loves little.” To her He said gently, “Your sins are forgiven… Your faith has saved you; go in peace.”

I watched her leave with a lightness in her step I had rarely seen. Her tears had been of sorrow turning to joy. Jesus’ words exposed Simon’s cold correctness and the woman’s grateful love, and in doing so they turned my whole understanding of God right way around. I had assumed people were forgiven because they first loved God enough; but Jesus showed it ran the other way—she loved much because she had been forgiven much, and Simon loved little because he imagined he had little to be forgiven. Her flood of love was not the price of her pardon but the proof of it. I felt convicted in my own heart. How much had I been forgiven? Did I love accordingly? Sitting in that room, I sensed Jesus seeing straight into each of us, not with condemnation but with truth that healed, inviting a deeper and more honest love.

These days with Him were steadily changing me. I saw power over death, mercy toward the doubtful, forgiveness for the broken. I felt more awake to my own need and more drawn to His kindness. Following Him meant walking in a light that revealed and restored at the same time—a light that showed me my sin only to wash it.

We continued moving through Galilee with Jesus, and a group of women began traveling with us as well—women who had been healed of evil spirits and infirmities. Among them was Mary, called Magdalene, from whom seven demons had gone out. She walked with a quiet dignity now, her presence steady and grateful. There was also Joanna, wife of Chuza, Herod’s household manager, and Susanna, and several others. These women provided for us out of their own resources, and I saw in them a devotion that humbled me. They listened to every teaching with focused attention, their faces often shining with relief and love. Being among them reminded me that the kingdom welcomed and restored hearts the world had given up on—that the same grace which had cast seven demons out of Mary now gave her back a dignity no one could take, and turned the rescued into the most devoted of all.

One day by the lake, a great crowd gathered again. Jesus got into a boat and sat down to teach, while the people stood on the shore. He told them many things in parables.
