I sat in the boat near Him, the gentle rocking of the water beneath us, and listened as He spoke of a sower going out to sow seed. Some fell along the path and was trampled or eaten by birds. Some fell on rock and sprang up but withered because it had no root. Some fell among thorns and was choked. But other seed fell on good soil and produced a crop a hundredfold. “He who has ears to hear, let him hear,” Jesus said. Later, when we were alone, we asked Him about the meaning. He explained patiently: the seed is the word of God, and the different soils represent different hearts. I felt the parable searching my own soul. The same good news, I realized, fell on every kind of heart, and what made the difference was not the seed but the soil that received it—so that even my believing was something to ask Him for, a softening of hard ground I could not work in myself. Was my heart good soil? I wanted it to be, and I began to pray that He would make it so.

He told other parables that day—the kingdom like a lamp set on a stand, not hidden under a bed; like a man who sows seed and then sleeps while it grows by itself; like a mustard seed that becomes the largest of garden plants. Each one opened my understanding a little more. I felt my mind stretching, my heart softening. The picture that lingered was the seed growing secretly while the farmer slept: the kingdom was not something I would build by my own striving but something God was quietly growing, from the smallest beginning, toward a harvest only He could bring. Sitting there with the other apostles, I experienced a growing sense of being let in on secrets of the kingdom hidden for ages—a quiet joy, mixed with awareness of how much I had been given.

That evening, after the crowds had gone, Jesus said to us, “Let us go across to the other side of the lake.” We set out in the boat while He fell asleep on a cushion in the stern. A fierce wind suddenly arose, and waves began breaking into the boat, filling it with water. The boat tossed violently. I gripped the side, my heart racing with fear as the water rose around my ankles. The other disciples shouted, waking Jesus: “Teacher, do you not care that we are perishing?” I felt the same panic—the wind howling, the waves crashing, the boat tilting dangerously. We had seen so many miracles, yet in that moment raw fear took hold, and I understood how quickly I still reached for terror instead of trust.

Jesus woke and rebuked the wind and the waves: “Peace! Be still!” At once the wind ceased, and there was a great calm. The water became smooth as glass. He looked at us and said, “Why are you so afraid? Have you still no faith?” I sat there, soaked and trembling, filled with both relief and a deeper awe. Who is this, that even the wind and sea obey Him? My fear turned to reverent wonder. The same word that forgave sins and raised the dead now governed the chaos of wind and water, and I saw that there was no realm—not sickness, not death, not the raging deep, not the storms within me—beyond the reach of His command. In the sudden stillness, with only the gentle lapping of water against the boat, I felt small yet safe, learning that to be saved was, in part, simply this: to be in the boat with Him and to trust that He cared.

We reached the other side, in the country of the Gerasenes. As soon as Jesus stepped out of the boat, a man with an unclean spirit met us. He lived among the tombs, wild and uncontrollable. Chains had not been able to bind him. He ran to Jesus and fell down before Him, crying out, “What have you to do with me, Jesus, Son of the Most High God? I adjure you by God, do not torment me.” The man’s eyes were tormented, his body marked by self-inflicted wounds. Jesus asked the spirit its name, and it answered, “Legion, for we are many.” After a brief exchange, Jesus commanded the spirits to come out. They entered a herd of pigs feeding nearby, and the herd rushed down the steep bank into the lake and drowned. He had crossed a whole stormy sea, it seemed, for this one ruined man whom no chain could hold—and what no chain could do, His word did in a moment.

The man was left sitting there, clothed and in his right mind. When the people of the region came and saw what had happened, they were afraid and begged Jesus to leave their region. The healed man wanted to follow us, but Jesus told him gently, “Go home to your friends and tell them how much the Lord has done for you, and how He has had mercy on you.” The man went away and began proclaiming what Jesus had done for him. I watched him go, amazed at the transformation. Here was the whole pattern again: a man in hopeless bondage, set free by a word, and then sent to tell of the mercy he had been shown. The first work He gave the rescued man was simply to testify to his rescue—and I understood that this was how the good news would travel, from one freed captive to the next. Being with Jesus meant seeing captivity turned to freedom even in places that feared and rejected the Liberator, and my own resolve to stay close deepened with every mile.

We crossed back over the lake, the water now calm and reflective under the sky. The boat moved steadily, the oars dipping with a quiet rhythm, and I sat near Jesus, still awestruck by the sudden stillness He had commanded. My clothes were damp, my body tired from the fear that had gripped me moments before, yet a new layer of trust was forming inside—like a root going deeper into soil I had not known was there. The other side felt familiar again as we approached Capernaum, the town’s lights beginning to appear in the gathering dusk.

As soon as we stepped ashore, a large crowd was waiting. They pressed around Jesus eagerly, voices overlapping in excitement and need. I stayed close to Him, helping to make a way through the people. Among them came Jairus, one of the rulers of the synagogue. He was a man of standing, yet in that moment he fell at Jesus’ feet, his face tight with desperation. “My little daughter is at the point of death,” he pleaded. “Come and lay your hands on her, so that she may be made well and live.” His voice broke with fatherly love and fear. Jesus agreed at once, and we began moving toward Jairus’ house. It struck me that a ruler of the synagogue and the demon-ridden man of the tombs had been brought to the very same place—on their faces before Him, with nothing to offer but their need. I walked just behind, sensing the urgency in the air, my own heart beating faster in sympathy for the man.

In the midst of the pressing crowd, a woman approached from behind. She had suffered from a flow of blood for twelve years—long years of isolation and exhaustion under the weight of her condition, unclean by the law and shut out from the worship of her people. She had spent all she had on physicians, yet only grew worse. Quietly, almost secretly, she reached out and touched the fringe of Jesus’ garment. I did not see it happen at first, but Jesus stopped suddenly and asked, “Who touched my garments?” The disciples looked around in confusion; the crowd was so dense it seemed impossible to know. But the woman, trembling with fear and hope, came forward and fell down before Him. She told Him the whole truth, her voice shaking. I watched her closely—her face worn yet filled with a fragile courage.

Jesus looked at her with kindness that seemed to wrap around her like a warm covering. “Daughter,” He said gently, “your faith has made you well. Go in peace, and be healed of your disease.” He would not let her slip away healed but unknown; He called her out so He could call her daughter—not merely mend her body but name her, restore her to a place among His people. At that moment she knew she was healed. I saw the relief flood her expression, her shoulders straightening as if a heavy burden had been lifted after twelve long years. Her quiet act of faith touched me deeply. In the chaos of the crowd, she had reached out in desperation and found mercy. It made me reflect on my own hesitations, my own need to reach for Him more boldly, trusting that even a trembling touch of faith would not go unanswered.

While Jesus was still speaking to her, messengers came from Jairus’ house with heavy news. “Your daughter is dead,” they told him. “Why trouble the Teacher any further?” Jairus’ face crumpled with grief. But Jesus turned to him immediately and said with calm strength, “Do not fear, only believe.” Those words steadied something in me as well—a quiet command to keep trusting precisely when everything said to give up. We continued on to the house, the atmosphere now thick with sorrow. At the door, there was already weeping and wailing. Jesus allowed only Peter, James, John, and me to go inside with Him and the girl’s parents.

Inside, the child lay on her bed—twelve years old, still and pale. The room felt heavy with finality. Jesus took her by the hand and said softly, “Talitha cumi,” which means, “Little girl, I say to you, arise.” Her eyes opened. She rose at once and began to walk. Her parents were overcome with amazement and joy, tears flowing freely. Jesus told them quietly to give her something to eat, showing care even in the miracle. I stood there, my breath caught in my throat, a profound sense of wonder filling me. Death had yielded again to His word, and this time I had been close enough to see His hand close around the cold little hand and warm it back to life. He spoke to death as gently as a mother wakes a sleeping child, and it obeyed Him. In that quiet room I felt the nearness of God in a way that left me hushed inside, certain that the One who could take death by the hand had come to do exactly that for all of us.

These events continued to shape me day by day. Each miracle revealed more of who He was, and each moment in His presence made me more aware of my own heart’s need for His touch. I followed Him with a deeper commitment, storing these things in my memory like treasures I would one day understand more fully—glimpses, I was beginning to sense, of a single great rescue He was moving toward, of which every healing was a foretaste.

We left Jairus’ house as the news of his daughter’s return to life began spreading through the streets of Capernaum like quiet ripples on the lake. I walked beside the others, my steps measured, my mind still replaying the moment Jesus took the girl’s small hand and spoke those gentle Aramaic words. The tenderness in His voice, the immediate response in her eyes as life returned—it lingered in me, stirring a mixture of awe and quiet introspection. I felt more aware than ever of how fragile life was, and how, in His hands, even death became something He could simply reach into and reverse.

In the days that followed, Jesus continued teaching and healing, but the pace was growing more demanding. The crowds seemed to multiply, drawn by reports of what He had done. One Sabbath He returned to His hometown of Nazareth. We entered the synagogue with Him, the familiar space filled with people who had known Him since childhood. I sat among the local men, watching their faces as Jesus stood to read and then began to teach. His words carried the same authority I had come to recognize, full of insight and truth. For a time the people listened with interest, murmuring about the wisdom He displayed.

But then the tone shifted. Someone whispered, “Is not this the carpenter, the son of Mary?” Others nodded, mentioning His brothers and sisters. I saw skepticism harden into offense on their faces. They could not reconcile the ordinary man they thought they knew with the power they had heard about. Jesus looked at them with quiet sadness and said, “A prophet is not without honor, except in his hometown and among his relatives and in his own house.” Their unbelief was so strong that He could do no mighty work there, except healing a few sick people by laying His hands on them. As we left Nazareth, I felt a heaviness in my chest. I had seen so much belief and transformation elsewhere; here, familiarity had blinded them. It taught me something sobering about the human heart—that salvation could come and stand in a man’s own synagogue, and he could shrug and call it the carpenter’s boy. The gift had to be received with the empty hands of faith, and these were too full of what they thought they already knew. Jesus’ calm acceptance of their rejection strengthened my own resolve to see Him clearly, beyond any preconceptions.

Not long after, Jesus called the twelve of us together. He gave us authority over unclean spirits and sent us out two by two. I went with one of the others, carrying nothing but a staff—no bread, no bag, no money. His instructions were clear: stay in one house where we were welcomed, shake the dust off our feet if a town would not receive us. We preached that people should repent, cast out demons, and anointed many sick with oil so they recovered. As we traveled from village to village, I felt a new sense of purpose and dependence. The mercy I had only watched Him pour out was now, by His authority, flowing through my own hands and words—not because I had become worthy of it, but because He had chosen to spread His rescue through ordinary, sent men. Speaking in His name, seeing lives touched, was both exhilarating and humbling. I returned to Jesus later with stories of what had happened, my heart full of gratitude for being entrusted with such work.

Around this time, reports reached us about John the Baptist. Herod had imprisoned him and, at the urging of Herodias, had him beheaded. When the disciples of John brought the news to Jesus, I saw a deep sorrow pass over His face. He had honored John publicly, calling him the greatest among those born of women. The death of the forerunner sent a cold thread of foreboding through me; if the one sent to prepare the way was cut down by the powers of this world, what would those powers do to the One he had prepared the way for? We withdrew for a time to a desolate place to rest, but the crowds followed. Seeing the great multitude, Jesus had compassion on them because they were like sheep without a shepherd—and I understood that this was what had drawn Him out of heaven in the first place: a shepherd coming after a flock that had no one to lead it home. He began teaching them many things.

As the day grew late, the disciples suggested sending the people away to buy food. But Jesus said, “You give them something to eat.” We had only five loaves and two fish. I watched as He took the bread and fish, looked up to heaven, blessed and broke them, then gave them to us to distribute. The food multiplied in His hands. I walked among the groups of fifty and a hundred, handing out pieces that never seemed to run out. Men, women, and children ate until they were satisfied. When we gathered the leftovers, there were twelve baskets full. I handled those fragments with care, my hands still amazed at what they had witnessed. Five thousand men, plus women and children, fed from so little. He took bread, blessed it, broke it, and gave it—and though I did not see it then, the same hands would soon take bread again, bless and break it, and call it His body given for us. In that moment I felt only a profound sense of abundance and care: Jesus provided not just enough, but more than enough, meeting the hunger of the crowds and the doubt of His followers alike with open-handed generosity. My heart swelled with worship and a deeper trust.

These experiences continued to form me. Each day with Jesus brought fresh revelations of His compassion, His authority, and His intimate knowledge of our hearts. I followed more closely, learning to trust even when the way seemed impossible, storing every memory like bread that would sustain me through whatever lay ahead.

We withdrew after the great feeding, but the crowds lingered with excitement, some even wanting to make Jesus king by force. He sent us ahead in the boat while He dismissed the people Himself. I climbed into the boat with the others as evening fell, the water dark and still beneath us. Jesus went up on the mountain alone to pray. I watched His figure grow smaller against the hillside until the gathering dusk hid Him. It struck me that the crowds wanted to seize Him and crown Him for the bread He gave, while He slipped away to pray—as if the kingdom He had come to bring could not be hurried into being by force, but only given in His own way and His own hour. Sitting at the oars, I felt a quiet reverence mixed with weariness. There was so much I did not yet understand about Him.

We rowed across the lake toward Capernaum. The wind rose suddenly, strong and contrary. Waves began to batter the boat, and we strained at the oars, our arms burning with effort. The darkness was thick, the boat rocking heavily. I gripped the wood tightly, my heart beating fast with the familiar fear that had gripped us before. We had rowed for hours, making little progress, when we saw something that stopped our breath—a figure walking on the water, coming toward us. It looked like a ghost in the dim light. Terror filled the boat. We cried out in alarm.

But then His voice reached us over the wind: “Take heart; it is I. Do not be afraid.” It was Jesus. My fear shifted at once into awe. Peter called out, “Lord, if it is you, command me to come to you on the water.” Jesus said, “Come.” Peter stepped out of the boat and began walking on the waves toward Him. For a few moments it seemed possible—his eyes fixed on Jesus. Then he looked at the wind and the waves, and doubt took him. He began to sink, crying, “Lord, save me!” Jesus reached out His hand immediately and caught him. “O you of little faith,” He said gently, “why did you doubt?” Together they climbed into the boat, and the wind ceased at once. The water grew calm around us. I have never forgotten the shortness of that prayer—“Lord, save me!”—three words gasped out by a sinking man, and the hand that caught him before he had even finished. I began to suspect that this was the whole of what any of us could do, and the whole of what He asked: to cry out as we went under, and to be caught.

We were all overcome. I knelt there in the boat, my clothes wet, my body trembling not just from cold but from the encounter. “Truly you are the Son of God,” we said to Him. In that moment, after the terror and the rescue, I felt a deeper surrender taking root in me. I had seen Him command storms before, but this—walking on the sea itself—revealed His mastery over creation in a new way. My heart was full of worship and a quiet awareness of my own frailty, and of how completely my safety lay not in my own grip on the boat but in His grip on me.

When we reached the land at Gennesaret, people recognized Him at once. They brought the sick on mats to the marketplaces, begging only to touch the fringe of His garment. And as many as touched it were made well. I moved among them, helping where I could, watching the steady flow of mercy. Even the faintest reach toward Him—a fingertip on the hem of His robe—was met with healing, as if no approach to Him in faith was ever too small to be answered. Each healing deepened the conviction growing inside me: this was no ordinary teacher.

Later, in Capernaum, the crowds found us again, still seeking Him after the feeding. Jesus taught in the synagogue there, and His words took a serious turn. “I am the bread of life,” He declared. “Your fathers ate the manna in the wilderness, and they died. This is the bread that comes down from heaven, so that one may eat of it and not die. I am the living bread that came down from heaven. If anyone eats of this bread, he will live forever. And the bread that I will give for the life of the world is my flesh.” The crowds had chased Him for another meal; He offered them Himself, and spoke for the first time so plainly of a body that would be given for the life of the world. I did not understand it, but I felt the ground of everything shift beneath the words—as though every loaf He had ever broken had been pointing here.

The people began to grumble. “How can this man give us his flesh to eat?” they asked. Even some of the disciples found it hard. Jesus did not soften the teaching. He spoke of eating His flesh and drinking His blood as the way to abide in Him and have life. Many turned away that day, walking no longer with Him. I watched them leave, feeling the weight of the moment. Jesus turned to the twelve of us and asked quietly, “Do you want to go away as well?” Simon Peter answered for us: “Lord, to whom shall we go? You have the words of eternal life, and we have believed, and have come to know, that you are the Holy One of God.”

His question searched me deeply. I felt the pull of the hard saying, yet something stronger held me—the recognition that life itself was in Him, and nowhere else. Where would I go? Back to a religion of washings and rules that could not reach the rot inside me, back to a world that ran out of wine and buried its only sons? There was no other well. In that synagogue, surrounded by the familiar smells of bread and oil lamps, I chose again to stay. My heart was committed, even when understanding lagged far behind.

After that difficult day in the synagogue at Capernaum, many who had followed Jesus turned back and no longer walked with Him. The air in the room felt heavier as they left, their footsteps echoing on the stone floor, voices murmuring in confusion and offense. I remained seated among the twelve, my hands resting on my knees, feeling the weight of the moment. Jesus’ words about His flesh and blood had tested us all. They were strange, even shocking, yet something in them rang with a truth I could not deny. When Peter spoke for us—“Lord, to whom shall we go? You have the words of eternal life”—I nodded inwardly. Those words became my own quiet resolution. I had seen too much, heard too much, tasted too deeply of the life He gave, to walk away now. My heart was bound to Him, even when my understanding faltered.

We left Capernaum and continued through Galilee, though Jesus no longer moved as openly. He taught us privately as we traveled, focusing on the deeper matters of the heart. One day some Pharisees and scribes from Jerusalem came to question Him. They noticed that some of us ate with hands that were not ceremonially washed according to the tradition of the elders. Their tone was sharp, accusatory. “Why do your disciples not walk according to the tradition of the elders, but eat with defiled hands?”

Jesus answered them directly, His voice steady and clear. He quoted the prophet Isaiah: “This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me; in vain do they worship me, teaching as doctrines the commandments of men.” Then He turned the challenge back on them, speaking of how they set aside God’s commandments for their own traditions—like the practice of Corban, where a person could declare resources devoted to God and thus avoid helping their parents. I listened closely, feeling the force of His words. He was exposing the difference between outward appearance and inner reality. It convicted me. How often had I focused on external rules while neglecting the weightier matters of justice, mercy, and faithfulness? His teaching felt like a mirror held up to my soul—uncomfortable, yet cleansing.

He called the crowd to Him again and said, “Hear me, all of you, and understand: there is nothing outside a person that by going into him can defile him, but the things that come out of a person are what defile him.” Later, when we were alone, He explained further: evil thoughts, sexual immorality, theft, murder, adultery, coveting, wickedness, deceit, sensuality, envy, slander, pride, foolishness—all these come from within and defile a person. The words sank into me deeply. I saw then why no amount of washing could ever make me clean: the defilement welled up from inside, from the heart itself, and no ritual could reach that far down. If I were ever to be made clean, it would have to be by someone who could remake the heart—and I was beginning to know who that someone was. Being near Jesus meant allowing Him to search the hidden places of my heart. There was no hiding, but also no rejection—only the call to be made new.

From Galilee we moved northward toward the region of Tyre and Sidon. Jesus seemed to want quieter time with us. A Syrophoenician woman, a Gentile, came seeking Him. Her daughter was severely oppressed by an unclean spirit. She begged Him for help, her voice full of desperate motherly love. At first Jesus was silent, testing the moment. The disciples urged Him to send her away. But she persisted, saying, “Yes, Lord; yet even the dogs under the table eat the children’s crumbs.” Her humility and faith moved Him. “For this saying,” He told her, “you may go your way; the demon has left your daughter.” When she returned home, she found her child well. I watched the exchange with growing respect. She had asked for nothing but a crumb, claiming no right to the children’s bread—and that very humility was the door her faith walked through. Jesus’ mercy reached past the borders of Israel to a Gentile mother who would take even the leftovers of grace, and it enlarged my own vision of how wide the kingdom would prove to be.

We returned through the Decapolis, and there people brought to Him a man who was deaf and had a speech impediment. They begged Jesus to lay His hand on him. Taking the man aside privately, away from the crowd, Jesus put His fingers into the man’s ears, spat and touched his tongue, then looked up to heaven, sighed, and said, “Ephphatha,” that is, “Be opened.” At once the man’s ears were opened, his tongue was released, and he spoke plainly. The people were astonished beyond measure. I stood nearby, witnessing the intimate care Jesus showed—drawing the man aside, using touch in a way that seemed so human, yet carried divine power. It moved me that the One who could speak galaxies into being stooped to put His own fingers in a deaf man’s ears, as if salvation always came this near, this personal.

These journeys and teachings continued to shape me. I felt myself changing—less quick to judge by outward appearances, more aware of the condition of the heart, more open to the breadth of God’s mercy. Following Jesus meant walking in growing light, even when the path included hard words and unexpected turns. My commitment to Him had become the central reality of my life.

That country has stayed with me, and the healing of the deaf man most of all, so let me tell it as I saw it up close. We had come back through the Decapolis after leaving the regions of Tyre and Sidon. The landscape opened up into a different world—ten Greek cities scattered across the hills and plains east of the Jordan and the Sea of Galilee. It was Gentile territory, more Hellenistic in feel than the villages of Galilee. Columns from pagan temples rose in the distance against the sky, and the air carried the faint scent of incense from distant altars mixed with the drier smell of pastureland and olive groves. The people here spoke Greek more readily, and their faces showed a blend of cultures—some with the sharper features of traders from the east, others tanned and sturdy like farmers of the Decapolis. It felt foreign to me, yet Jesus moved through it with the same steady purpose He carried everywhere. Being in this region reminded me how far His reach already extended, beyond the familiar boundaries of Israel—into the very places we had been taught to count as outside the mercy of God.

The crowds found us again, bringing the sick and the broken. The deaf man stands out in my memory above the rest. His speech was so impaired he could barely make understandable sounds. His friends led him forward, their eyes pleading as they begged Jesus to lay a hand on him. Jesus did not heal him in the open press of the crowd. Instead, He took the man aside privately, away from the noise and staring eyes. I followed at a short distance and watched closely.

Jesus put His fingers into the man’s ears, then spat and touched the man’s tongue with the moisture. It was an intimate, almost earthy gesture—human and direct. Then He looked up to heaven, sighed deeply as if carrying the man’s burden in His own spirit, and spoke one clear word: “Ephphatha.” That is, “Be opened.” At once the man’s ears were opened. His face changed in an instant—eyes widening as sound flooded in. His tongue loosened, and he began speaking plainly, words tumbling out with growing excitement. I stood there, my own breath catching, feeling a surge of holy wonder move through me. That sigh stayed with me longest: He did not heal at arm’s length but seemed to take the man’s closed-up silence into Himself before He opened it, as though every rescue cost Him something. Jesus had not needed dramatic displays; a touch, a sigh, a word—and barriers that had shut a man off from the world fell away. I felt humbled witnessing it, aware again of how much I myself needed opening in places I could not reach on my own.

The people were astonished beyond measure. They brought more and more to Him—lame, blind, crippled, mute—and He healed them all. For three days the crowd stayed with us, listening to His teaching and receiving His care. Their faces, once marked by pain and isolation, began to shine with hope. I moved among them, helping distribute what little we had, my heart full with a growing sense of the kingdom’s reach. This was not only for Israel. Here in the Decapolis, among Gentiles who had known other gods and other ways, Jesus was revealing the mercy of the true God—and I remembered the Samaritan well, and the centurion, and the Gentile mother content with crumbs, and saw that they were all of a piece. The Savior of the world had meant exactly that.

When the three days drew to a close and the people grew hungry, Jesus called us aside. “I have compassion on the crowd,” He said, “because they have been with me now three days and have nothing to eat. And I am unwilling to send them away hungry, lest they faint on the way.” We had only seven loaves and a few small fish. The memory of the earlier feeding near Capernaum was still fresh, yet we still struggled to believe. Jesus took the bread, gave thanks, broke it, and gave it to us to distribute. Once again, the food multiplied in His hands. I walked among the groups, handing out pieces that never seemed to end. Four thousand men ate, along with women and children, until all were satisfied. When we gathered the leftovers, there were seven baskets full. He had broken bread for the children of Israel on the green grass of Galilee; now He broke it just the same for a hungry Gentile crowd in pagan country. The same blessed, broken bread, given to outsiders—His grace kept the same shape no matter whose hands received it.

After this, He sent the crowds away and got into the boat with us, heading back toward the western shore. As I sat in the boat watching the Decapolis hills recede behind us, I reflected on all I had seen. The region had shown me that the life He carried was not confined to one people or place. My spirit felt enlarged, my commitment to Him deepened. Every new place, every new healing, was slowly teaching me that the salvation He brought was meant for the whole world, and that following Him meant being willing to go wherever that salvation needed to be carried.

We sailed back across the lake from the Decapolis, the boat moving steadily under a quiet sky. The hills on the eastern shore slowly faded behind us, their pagan temples and open plains giving way once more to the familiar shoreline of Galilee. I sat near the stern, the gentle rocking of the water beneath me, my mind still turning over the days we had spent among the Gentiles. The abundance of the seven loaves, the healed man speaking clearly for the first time, the astonished faces of the crowd—all of it settled deep in me like a quiet confirmation. Jesus’ mercy was wider than I had imagined.

When we reached the other side and came to Dalmanutha, the Pharisees and Sadducees soon found us. They approached as a group, their robes clean and their expressions tight with challenge. “Give us a sign from heaven,” they demanded, “to prove you are who you claim.” Their voices carried suspicion and a desire to test Him. I watched Jesus closely. He sighed, a sound heavy with sorrow rather than anger, and answered them, “Why does this generation seek a sign? Truly, no sign will be given to this generation.” He turned away from them without further words. I felt the tension in the air, the growing opposition that seemed to follow us now like a shadow. It troubled me that men could stand in the presence of the Savior, watch Him heal and feed thousands, and still demand He prove Himself—as if the trouble were never the lack of evidence but a heart unwilling to come.

We got back into the boat and crossed once more. As we rowed, Jesus warned us, “Watch out; beware of the leaven of the Pharisees and the leaven of Herod.” We thought He was speaking about bread, since we had forgotten to bring any. But He knew our discussion and gently rebuked us: “Why are you discussing the fact that you have no bread? Do you not yet perceive or understand? Are your hearts hardened? Having eyes, do you not see, and having ears, do you not hear?” His words pierced me. He reminded us of the two feedings—the five thousand and the four thousand—and how much was left over each time. Slowly it dawned on us that He was warning against the teaching of the Pharisees, a subtle corruption of self-righteousness that could spread silently like yeast through a whole loaf. I sat quietly after that, recognizing in myself how easily I could be soured by the very pride that refused to come to Him empty-handed. His patience with us, even in our slowness, stirred a deeper affection in my heart.

We came to Bethsaida. There, some people brought a blind man to Jesus and begged Him to touch him. Jesus took the man by the hand and led him out of the village, away from the noise. I followed at a respectful distance and watched. He spat on the man’s eyes, laid His hands on him, and asked, “Do you see anything?” The man looked up and said, “I see people, but they look like trees walking.” His sight was partial, unclear. Jesus laid His hands on him once more. Then the man’s eyes were opened fully, and he saw everything clearly. Jesus sent him home, telling him not to enter the village. I stood there, moved by the tenderness of the healing—the gradual restoration, the patient second touch. It mirrored my own slow seeing exactly: I, too, had glimpsed Him in blurred and partial ways, mistaking trees for men, and I, too, needed His hand to come back again and again before I could see who He truly was. Gratitude filled me, and a quiet humility that He did not grow weary of touching half-blind eyes a second time.

From there we traveled north toward the region of Caesarea Philippi. The hills grew steeper, the air cooler as we climbed. One day, when we were alone with Him, Jesus asked us, “Who do people say that I am?” We answered with the various opinions we had heard—John the Baptist, Elijah, one of the prophets. Then He looked at us directly and asked, “But who do you say that I am?” Peter answered without hesitation, his voice strong: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.” I felt something shift inside me as the words were spoken. They gathered up everything I had seen since the Jordan—the Lamb, the wine, the new birth, the forgiven sins, the bread of life, the wind made still, the dead raised—into a single confession. This was who He was. Jesus blessed Peter, speaking of the rock and the church He would build, and of the keys of the kingdom. The moment carried a weight and a glory I could scarcely take in.

Yet right after, Jesus began to teach us plainly that He must go to Jerusalem, suffer many things, be killed, and rise again on the third day. The words stunned me. We had just confessed Him the Christ, the Son of the living God—and the first thing He told us about the Christ was that He would be killed. Peter even pulled Him aside to rebuke Him, but Jesus turned and said, “Get behind me, Satan! You are a hindrance to me. For you are not setting your mind on the things of God, but on the things of man.” I felt shaken. The rebuke was sharp because the temptation was real: every part of me, like Peter, wanted a Christ who would conquer, not one who would die. Yet there was no mistaking how firmly Jesus set His face toward it. The death was not a tragedy that might befall Him; it was the very thing He had come to do, the road to which all the rest had been leading. My heart wrestled with fear and confusion, yet underneath it the conviction held: this was the One we had waited for, and if His way ran through suffering, then suffering must somehow be the shape of our rescue.

We continued northward into the region near Caesarea Philippi, the hills rising higher and the air growing cooler as we walked. The pagan temples and shrines to false gods dotted the landscape in the distance, a constant reminder of the spiritual darkness that still covered much of the world. Yet Jesus moved among it all with quiet confidence, as though He carried a light no shadow could overcome. He told us plainly that if anyone would come after Him, he must deny himself, take up his cross, and follow—that whoever sought to save his life would lose it, but whoever lost his life for His sake would find it. The words landed heavily so soon after His talk of suffering and death. I began to see that the cross He was walking toward was not His alone to carry; the life He gave would reshape ours into the same cross-bearing pattern, and that losing everything to follow Him was, strangely, the only way to gain anything that lasted. Six days after Peter’s confession, Jesus took Peter, James, John, and me up a high mountain to pray. The climb was steady, the path rocky beneath our sandals, but being with Him made the effort feel purposeful. My legs tired, yet my spirit felt drawn upward, expectant without knowing why.

As the evening deepened, Jesus took Peter, James, and John and began to climb a high mountain alone with them to pray. The rest of us He left at the foot of it, and we made a rough camp among the rocks below, watching the three figures grow smaller against the darkening slope until the night swallowed them entirely. I remember the strange ache of being left behind, the longing to follow tangled together with a quiet trust that He knew what He was doing. We kept a low fire and spoke little. The mountain loomed over us, black against the stars, and once or twice I thought I saw a faint light high on the heights, though I could not say whether it was the moon on bare stone or something I had no word for. None of us slept easily that night.

It was not until they came down that we learned what had happened up there, and Peter could hardly tell it without his voice shaking. He said that as Jesus prayed, the appearance of His face had changed and begun to shine like the sun, and His clothing turned a dazzling white, whiter than anyone on earth could bleach it. While the three of them stared, two men appeared and stood speaking with Him—Moses and Elijah, the law and the prophets themselves—and they spoke with Him of His departure, which He was about to accomplish at Jerusalem. Peter admitted, almost ashamed, that he had blurted out an offer to put up three shelters, one for each of them, not knowing what he was saying, for they were terrified. John told the rest of it more quietly. A bright cloud had come and overshadowed them, he said, and out of the cloud a voice had spoken: “This is my beloved Son, my Chosen One; listen to Him.” At the sound of it the three had fallen on their faces in dread, until Jesus came and touched them and said, “Rise, and have no fear.” When they lifted their eyes, He was standing alone again, just as they had always known Him.

They told us these things in low voices as we walked, for Jesus had charged the three to tell no one what they had seen until the Son of Man had risen from the dead. We turned that last phrase over among ourselves, uncertain what rising He meant, and why glory and suffering should be spoken in the same breath. But the thing that lodged deepest in me was what Moses and Elijah had come to discuss with Him: not His glory, but His departure—His death at Jerusalem. The law and the prophets had stood in blazing light only to speak of the cross, as if the whole of Scripture had always been leaning toward that one dark hour, and the radiant Son had come down the mountain precisely in order to die. I had not stood inside that cloud, and some part of me wished that I had; yet hearing it from them, watching the awe still trembling in their faces, was its own kind of witness. The Jesus who walked the dusty road at my side, who would soon eat with us and sleep beneath the same open sky, was the very One whose face had blazed like the noon sun—and that One was walking, on purpose, toward His death for us. I walked the rest of the way in silence, carrying a glory I had only heard described, and somehow it steadied me for the road ahead.

Even before they had come down from the mountain, a large crowd had gathered around the rest of us at its foot. A man came forward out of the crowd, his face etched with desperation. He had brought his only son, who was severely afflicted by an unclean spirit. The boy would suddenly cry out, foam at the mouth, grind his teeth, and be thrown to the ground in violent convulsions. The father had begged us to cast it out, but we could not, and some scribes had begun to argue with us while the crowd looked on; I felt the sting of our helplessness keenly. When Jesus came down and saw the commotion, the father turned to Him and pleaded, “If you can do anything, have compassion on us and help us.” Jesus replied with both challenge and invitation: “If you can believe, all things are possible to one who believes.” The father cried out with tears, “I believe; help my unbelief!”

That cry became one of my own truest prayers, for I heard my whole heart in it. The man did not pretend to a faith he did not have, nor did he give up for lack of it; he brought even his unbelief to Jesus and asked Him to mend it. I saw in that moment that faith itself was not a coin I produced to purchase healing, but a gift I could ask for from the very One I was struggling to trust. I watched as Jesus rebuked the unclean spirit, commanding it to come out and never enter the boy again. The spirit cried out and convulsed the boy violently one last time before leaving him. The child lay still, as if dead, but Jesus took him by the hand and lifted him up, and he stood whole. The crowd was amazed. Later, when we were alone, the disciples asked Jesus why they had failed. He told them, “This kind cannot be driven out by anything but prayer.” His answer humbled me again. Set side by side—the glory the three had seen on the heights, and the failure we had just met at the foot of the mountain—these showed me that our own strength was never the point; the rescue was His, and it came down to us through dependence, not ability. My heart remained fixed on Him, even as the road toward Jerusalem began to feel heavier with unspoken cost.

We continued our journey, moving more privately now through Galilee. Jesus wanted to avoid the crowds for a time, for He was teaching us the deeper things that lay ahead. As we walked the familiar roads between villages, the sun warm on our shoulders and the scent of olive groves and grain fields around us, He began speaking plainly once more: “The Son of Man is going to be delivered into the hands of men, and they will kill Him, and when He is killed, after three days He will rise.”

The words fell on us heavily. I walked just behind Him, my sandals pressing into the dusty path, and felt a coldness settle in my stomach despite the warmth of the day. We did not understand what He meant, and we were afraid to ask Him. A quiet fear gripped my heart—not the holy awe of the mountain, but a deeper dread. Yet I noticed that He spoke of being killed and of rising again in the same breath, the way Moses and Elijah had joined glory and departure on the mountain; and somewhere beneath my fear a small, stubborn hope began to grow that the death He kept naming was not the end of the story but the heart of it. I had seen too many impossible things to doubt His power, even if I could not yet grasp why power should choose to suffer.

We returned to Capernaum and gathered in the house where we often stayed. The familiar smell of baked bread and fish lingered in the air. Some tax collectors approached Peter at the door, asking, “Does your teacher not pay the temple tax?” Peter answered quickly that He did. When he came inside, Jesus spoke to him first: “What do you think, Simon? From whom do kings of the earth take toll or tax? From their sons or from others?” Peter replied, “From others.” Jesus nodded. “Then the sons are free. However, not to give offense to them, go to the sea and cast a hook, and take the first fish that comes up. Open its mouth and you will find a shekel. Take that and give it to them for me and for yourself.”

I listened in quiet amazement as Peter later returned with the coin exactly as Jesus had said. The ordinary and the miraculous wove together so naturally in His presence. But what stayed with me was the heart of His question: as the Son of the Temple’s God He owed nothing, He was free—yet He chose to place Himself under the tax all the same. I was beginning to see a pattern in Him that I could not yet name: the One who owed nothing kept putting Himself under what He did not owe, for the sake of others. He was Lord even over the fish in the sea and the laws of men, yet again and again He stepped beneath them.

Later that same day, an argument arose among us. We had been discussing who was the greatest in the kingdom. The question had started innocently enough on the road but had grown heated. Jesus knew our thoughts. He sat down, called us to Him, and took a little child in His arms. The child stood quietly against Him, small and trusting. Jesus said, “Whoever receives one such child in my name receives me, and whoever receives me receives not me but Him who sent me.” Then He added, “If anyone would be first, he must be last of all and servant of all.”

His words cut through our pride like a clean blade. I felt ashamed as I looked at the child’s innocent face. We had been striving for position, yet Jesus pointed us toward humility and service. And I could not help seeing that He was describing Himself: the One who was first of all had made Himself last of all, the Lord becoming servant, even now setting His face toward the lowest place of all on a cross. The greatness of the kingdom ran in exactly the opposite direction from the greatness of the world, and the road down was the road He Himself was walking to save us. I resolved in my heart to learn this way, even though I knew it would be difficult.

John then spoke up about something that had been bothering him. “Teacher, we saw someone casting out demons in your name, and we tried to stop him, because he was not following us.” Jesus replied gently but firmly, “Do not stop him, for no one who does a mighty work in my name will be able soon afterward to speak evil of me. For the one who is not against us is for us.” The answer broadened my understanding once more. The kingdom was larger than our small circle, and its saving power was not ours to hoard. Jealousy had no place in it.

These teachings settled deeply into me as we prepared to move toward Jerusalem. The road ahead felt more solemn now. I walked with a quieter spirit, storing His words like treasure, aware that following Him meant laying down my pride, my fears, and my limited understanding. Yet in His presence, even the hard lessons carried hope. He was leading us, and I would continue to follow, step by step, wherever the path took us.

We remained in Capernaum a little longer, the familiar rhythm of life by the lake continuing around us while everything within us felt increasingly unsettled. One evening in the house, after the children had been sent to bed and the oil lamps burned low, Peter came to Jesus with a question that had been weighing on him. “Lord,” he asked, “how often will my brother sin against me, and I forgive him? As many as seven times?”

Jesus looked at him with that steady, penetrating gaze I had come to know so well. “I do not say to you seven times, but seventy-seven times.” Then He told us a parable about a king who settled accounts with his servants. One servant owed an enormous debt—ten thousand talents—and begged for patience. The king, moved with compassion, forgave the entire debt. But that same servant went out and seized a fellow servant who owed him only a hundred denarii, refusing to show the same mercy. The king’s anger burned when he heard of it, and he delivered the unforgiving servant to the jailers until the debt was paid.

As Jesus finished the story, the room was quiet except for the soft crackle of the lamps. I felt the parable sink like a stone into deep water inside me. How easily I could see myself in that first servant—owing a debt I could never repay in a hundred lifetimes, forgiven it all out of sheer compassion, and then turning to choke a brother over some trifling hundred denarii. I understood for the first time that this was the whole arithmetic of the kingdom: I had been forgiven an unpayable debt, and every grudge I clung to was a refusal to let that mercy flow through me. A heart that had truly received such pardon could not hold its own pardons back; if it did, it showed it had never grasped the size of what it had been given. I sat there, hands folded, letting the truth work its way deeper, grateful for the gentle yet firm way He taught us.

Not many days later, we left Capernaum and set our faces toward Jerusalem. The road south was well-traveled, winding through the hills of Samaria. The air grew warmer as we descended, carrying the scent of ripening figs and dust from the dry paths. Jesus sent messengers ahead to prepare the way, but when we entered a Samaritan village, the people would not receive us because our faces were set toward Jerusalem. The rejection stung. James and John, their tempers flaring like the “sons of thunder” they were, turned to Jesus and asked, “Lord, do you want us to tell fire to come down from heaven and consume them?” Their zeal was fierce, but Jesus turned and rebuked them. “You do not know what manner of spirit you are of; for the Son of Man came not to destroy people’s lives but to save them.”

I walked beside them afterward in silence, turning that sentence over and over: the Son of Man came not to destroy but to save. It was as plain a statement of His whole purpose as I had ever heard, and it cut against everything in me that wanted Him to call down fire on those who spurned Him. He was bent on rescue, not ruin—even toward a village that had just shut its door in His face. The road felt heavier after that, the dust clinging more stubbornly to our robes, yet His presence remained the steady center that kept us moving forward, and I held that one word close: He had come to save.

Later, Jesus appointed seventy-two others and sent them on ahead of Him, two by two, into every town and place where He Himself was about to go. I watched as they received their instructions: “The harvest is plentiful, but the laborers are few. Pray therefore the Lord of the harvest to send out laborers into His harvest.” They were to take nothing for the journey—no money bag, no sandals, no staff—and to heal the sick and proclaim that the kingdom of God had come near. As they departed in pairs along different roads, I felt a stirring of both excitement and responsibility. The work was expanding beyond the twelve of us. The harvest He spoke of was a field full of people to be gathered home, and He was sending laborers out into it ahead of His own coming—as if the saving He did could never be content to stay in one pair of hands.

When the seventy-two returned, their faces were alight with joy. “Lord,” they said, “even the demons are subject to us in your name!” Jesus rejoiced in the Holy Spirit and praised the Father for hiding these things from the wise and revealing them to little children. Then He turned to us and said privately, “Blessed are the eyes that see what you see! For many prophets and kings desired to see what you see, and did not see it.” He told the seventy-two not to rejoice chiefly that the spirits obeyed them, but that their names were written in heaven—and I understood that the greatest wonder was never the power that flowed through us but the mercy that had claimed us, our names kept safe in heaven by grace we had not earned.

Hearing those words filled me with a profound sense of privilege. I had walked with Him, heard from the three of the glory on the mountain, witnessed countless healings, heard teachings that would echo through the ages. Yet the road to Jerusalem now carried an undercurrent of gathering storm clouds. My heart held both gratitude and growing apprehension. Being with Jesus meant embracing the joy of the kingdom while also preparing for the cost—His cost, I was beginning to fear, more than ours. I continued to follow, step by step, storing every moment in my heart like seeds for a future harvest I could not yet fully see.

We pressed on toward Jerusalem, the road growing more crowded with pilgrims as the days passed. One afternoon, as the sun beat down on the dusty path lined with rocky hills and scattered olive trees, a lawyer stood up to test Jesus. His voice carried the careful precision of one trained in the law: “Teacher, what shall I do to inherit eternal life?”

Jesus answered by turning the question back to him: “What is written in the Law? How do you read it?” The lawyer replied smoothly, “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your strength and with all your mind, and your neighbor as yourself.” Jesus nodded and said, “You have answered correctly; do this, and you will live.” I noticed He did not soften the law’s demand in the least—do this, and you will live—as if to let the man feel the full, impossible weight of a love he had never once managed to give.

But the man, wanting to justify himself, asked further, “And who is my neighbor?” Jesus then told a story that has stayed with me ever since. A man was going down from Jerusalem to Jericho and fell among robbers. They stripped him, beat him, and left him half dead on the side of the road. A priest came by, saw him, and passed on the other side. Then a Levite came to the place, looked, and passed by as well. But a Samaritan—a man from the people we often despised—came upon him. When he saw the wounded man, he had compassion. He bound up his wounds, pouring on oil and wine, set him on his own animal, brought him to an inn, and took care of him. The next day he gave the innkeeper two denarii and promised to repay whatever more was spent.

Jesus looked at the lawyer and asked, “Which of these three, do you think, proved to be a neighbor to the man who fell among the robbers?” The lawyer answered quietly, “The one who showed mercy on him.” Jesus said simply, “Go and do likewise.”

I walked beside the others, the story working its way into my heart like good medicine. The Samaritan—unexpected, even unwelcome in our eyes—had become the true neighbor, spending his own oil and wine and silver on a stranger left for dead. The longer I carried the picture, the more it seemed to me a portrait of the Lord Himself: the despised One who comes to the very people who scorn Him, finds us robbed and beaten and half dead by the road, and pays out of His own purse the whole cost of our healing. The lawyer had asked what he must do to inherit eternal life; Jesus showed him a love so costly that no one keeps it—no one, except the One telling the story. I felt a quiet conviction stirring within me, and beneath it a deeper wonder at the Neighbor who had stopped for me.

Not long after, we came to a village where a woman named Martha welcomed us into her home. She was busy with much serving—preparing food, moving quickly between tasks, her face flushed with effort. Her sister Mary sat at Jesus’ feet, listening to His teaching. Martha, growing frustrated, came and said, “Lord, do you not care that my sister has left me to serve alone? Tell her to help me.”

Jesus answered with gentleness but clarity: “Martha, Martha, you are anxious and troubled about many things, but one thing is necessary. Mary has chosen the good portion, which will not be taken away from her.”

I watched the exchange carefully. Martha’s diligence was good, yet Mary had grasped what mattered most: before anything could be done for Him, something had first to be received from Him. The one thing necessary was Jesus Himself—to sit at His feet and take in His words. I felt the gentle correction land on my own restless heart, which was always readier to work for Him than to receive from Him. In the simple house, with its smell of baking bread and herbs, I learned again that all true service must flow out of having first sat still and let Him fill me.

These teachings traveled with me as we moved onward. The road to Jerusalem now felt both urgent and solemn. Every parable, every correction, every moment in His presence was shaping me further, stripping away old ways of thinking and replacing them with the realities of the kingdom. My spirit remained attentive and yielded, walking step by step with the One whose words carried both challenge and life.

We continued our journey southward, the hills of Judea rising gradually before us as we drew nearer to Jerusalem. The air grew drier, carrying the sharp scent of wild thyme crushed under our sandals and the distant smoke of cooking fires from villages nestled in the valleys. One evening, after a long day of walking, we stopped in a place where Jesus often went apart to pray. We found Him there again, alone for a time, kneeling in the fading light. When He finished, one of us asked Him, “Lord, teach us to pray, as John taught his disciples.”

Jesus sat with us under the gathering stars and gave us words that have since become the very breath of my life: “When you pray, say: Father, hallowed be your name. Your kingdom come. Give us each day our daily bread, and forgive us our sins, for we ourselves forgive everyone who is indebted to us. And lead us not into temptation.” The first word undid me—Father. He was teaching us to speak to the Most High the way He spoke to Him, as if His own sonship were being opened to make room for us, as if the whole point of the rescue were to bring beggars and sinners into a family and let us call God by that name. And the forgiveness of our sins sat right in the middle of it, asked for daily, as plainly as bread.

The simplicity of it moved me deeply. No long, elaborate phrases—just a child speaking to a Father. I felt my own prayers, which had often been wordy and anxious, grow quieter within me. He continued teaching: “Ask, and it will be given to you; seek, and you will find; knock, and it will be opened to you.” His voice was low and steady in the cool night air. I sat close, feeling the weight of His words press gently against my heart. Prayer was not a performance, but relationship—persistent, trusting, humble—the speech of children newly brought home. In that moment, with the soft wind stirring the grass around us, I sensed my spirit being reshaped once more, drawn closer to the Father through the Son.

The following days brought fresh challenges. We were in a house when Jesus cast out a demon that had made a man mute. The man spoke immediately, and the crowd marveled. But some accused Him, saying, “He casts out demons by Beelzebul, the prince of demons.” Others demanded a sign from heaven. Jesus answered them with calm authority, explaining that a kingdom divided against itself cannot stand. “But if it is by the finger of God that I cast out demons,” He said, “then the kingdom of God has come upon you.”

I listened with my whole being, feeling both the power of His words and the growing resistance around us. His presence always seemed to draw a line—some were drawn closer in faith, others pulled away in offense. It struck me that there was no neutral ground near Him: the same finger of God that set captives free hardened those determined not to come. Later, when the crowds had thinned, He warned us about an unclean spirit returning with worse companions to a house left empty and swept. The teaching settled in my chest with sober weight: it was not enough to be cleansed of an old evil; the swept house had to be filled, and only His own life and presence could fill it. To be saved was not merely to be emptied of sin but to be inhabited by Him.

As we traveled on, Jesus spoke more openly about the cost of following Him. “Foxes have holes, and birds of the air have nests,” He said to one eager man who wanted to follow, “but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay His head.” To another who asked to bury his father first, Jesus replied, “Leave the dead to bury their own dead. But as for you, go and proclaim the kingdom of God.” The words were sharp, yet spoken with love. I felt their edge in my own soul. Following Him meant everything else becoming secondary—not because the kingdom was a hard bargain, but because He was a treasure worth more than all I would lay down for Him. My old life—comforts, obligations, securities—seemed increasingly distant, like shadows fading in strong sunlight.

These moments on the road were etching themselves into me. Each teaching, each healing, each quiet conversation under the open sky was slowly transforming the way I saw the world. My heart remained full—awed by His authority, humbled by His demands, and strangely at peace in His company. The path toward Jerusalem stretched ahead, more serious now, yet I walked it willingly, step by steady step, with the One who had become the center of my existence.

We drew closer to Jerusalem, the holy city now appearing on the horizon like a crown set upon the hills. The roads were busier, filled with pilgrims making their way for the coming feasts. I walked with a growing awareness of the weight upon Jesus’ shoulders, though His step remained steady and unhurried. One day, as we rested under the shade of a spreading tree, He spoke again of the coming trials. “Behold, we are going up to Jerusalem, and everything that is written about the Son of Man by the prophets will be accomplished. For He will be delivered over to the Gentiles and will be mocked and shamefully treated and spit upon. And after flogging Him, they will kill Him, and on the third day He will rise.”

The words landed heavily among us. I felt a tightness in my chest, a mingling of dread and confusion. How could this be? The One who calmed storms, raised the dead, and shone with divine glory on the mountain—how could He speak so calmly of suffering and death? Yet He kept saying it was written, that the prophets had marked out this very road long before, and that He was not being dragged toward Jerusalem but going up to it on purpose. I looked at His face and saw both sorrow and resolve there, like a man who saw the full path ahead and still chose to walk it for reasons I could not yet fathom. I did not understand, but I trusted. My love for Him had grown beyond fear now; it had become the ground I stood on.

We arrived in the region near Jerusalem, and the tension in the air was unmistakable. Many were talking about Him in quiet corners and along the roads. Some said He was a good man; others said He was leading people astray. Jesus went up to the Feast of Tabernacles, not openly at first, but in a more hidden way. When He finally began teaching in the Temple courts, the people were astonished. “How is it that this man has learning, when He has never studied?” they asked. Jesus answered, “My teaching is not mine, but His who sent me. If anyone’s will is to do God’s will, he will know whether the teaching is from God or whether I am speaking on my own authority.”

I stood in the outer court, the marble stones cool beneath my feet, the voices of merchants and worshippers echoing around the colonnades. I watched the faces of those listening—some angry, some intrigued, some afraid. The religious leaders sent officers to arrest Him, but they returned empty-handed, saying, “No one ever spoke like this man!” The power in His words was undeniable. They reached into the heart and exposed what was there—and I saw that a man’s response to those words was never really about the words at all, but about whether he was willing to do the will of God or determined to keep his own.

One morning, as the sun rose higher and light flooded the Temple, the scribes and Pharisees brought a woman caught in adultery and set her before Him. She stood trembling, her head bowed in shame. They asked Jesus what should be done, reminding Him of the law that she should be stoned. I felt the trap they were laying. Jesus bent down and wrote with His finger on the ground. Then He stood and said, “Let him who is without sin among you be the first to throw a stone at her.” One by one, beginning with the older ones, they dropped their stones and left until only the woman remained. Jesus looked at her with kindness and said, “Woman, where are they? Has no one condemned you?” She answered, “No one, Lord.” He replied gently, “Neither do I condemn you; go, and from now on sin no more.”

I felt the mercy in that moment like a cool wind on a hot day. The woman’s relief was visible—her shoulders softened, her eyes lifted with new hope. He had not pretended her sin was nothing; He told her plainly to leave it. Yet He sent her away forgiven rather than condemned, and only later did I understand the cost of it: the condemnation she had earned did not simply vanish. The One who refused to throw the stone would Himself, before long, stand condemned in her place. His mercy was never cheap; it was being charged, even then, to His own account. It stirred deep gratitude in me, along with a fresh awareness of my own need for that same mercy.

As the feast continued, Jesus taught boldly in the Temple. “I am the light of the world,” He declared. “Whoever follows me will not walk in darkness, but will have the light of life.” The words rang through the courts with authority. Some believed, but others grew angrier, picking up stones to throw at Him. Yet His hour had not yet come, and He slipped away. I followed close behind, my heart pounding from the nearness of danger, yet more convinced than ever that He was the One sent from the Father. He had named Himself the light of the world, and I could see the proof in the very crowd around Him: the same light that gave the light of life to those who followed drove those who loved the dark into a fury. Being with Him in Jerusalem felt like standing at the very center of God’s story—holy, dangerous, and full of life. My spirit was quiet but resolute. I would stay with Him, no matter what the coming days would bring.

We remained in Jerusalem as the Feast of Tabernacles drew to a close, the city still buzzing with pilgrims and the lingering scent of leafy booths and incense hanging in the air. One Sabbath, as we walked along a street near the Temple, we passed a man who had been blind from birth. He sat begging by the roadside, his eyes clouded and unseeing, his hands outstretched in quiet desperation. The disciples asked Jesus, “Rabbi, who sinned, this man or his parents, that he was born blind?”

Jesus answered with a gentleness that cut through our assumptions: “It was not that this man sinned, or his parents, but that the works of God might be displayed in him. We must work the works of Him who sent me while it is day; night is coming, when no one can work. As long as I am in the world, I am the light of the world.” I had assumed the man’s darkness was a verdict on someone’s sin; Jesus saw it instead as a place for the mercy of God to be put on display. It made me wonder how much of what I counted as judgment was waiting, in His hands, to become a showcase for grace.

I stood nearby, watching closely. Jesus spat on the ground, made mud with the saliva, and spread it on the man’s eyes. The blind man did not flinch or pull away; there was a quiet trust in his posture. Jesus then told him, “Go, wash in the pool of Siloam.” The man rose and felt his way along the street toward the pool, his steps uncertain but determined. I followed at a distance with the others, my heart beating with expectation. When he returned, his eyes were open—clear, seeing, filled with wonder as he looked around at the world for the first time. Colors, faces, the brightness of the sky—he drank it all in with speechless joy. The change in him was immediate and undeniable. People who had known him as the blind beggar began murmuring, some saying it was the same man, others insisting it was only someone like him. But he kept declaring, “I am the man.”

The Pharisees soon heard of it and brought the healed man before them for questioning. I stood in the outer court, listening as the interrogation unfolded. Their voices were sharp with suspicion. They asked how he had received his sight, and when he told them about the mud and the washing, they divided among themselves. Some said Jesus could not be from God because He had made mud on the Sabbath. Others wondered how a sinner could do such signs. They called in the man’s parents, who confirmed he had been born blind but nervously distanced themselves from how he was healed, fearing the leaders. Then they questioned the man again, pressing him harshly. His answer grew bolder: “One thing I do know, that though I was blind, now I see.” Finally, in quiet defiance, he said, “If this man were not from God, he could do nothing.”

They cast him out. I watched him leave, his shoulders straight despite the rejection. Later, Jesus found him and asked, “Do you believe in the Son of Man?” The man answered with humble longing, “Who is he, sir, that I may believe in him?” Jesus replied, “You have seen him, and it is he who is speaking to you.” The man fell down before Him and worshiped. In that moment, I felt a deep stirring in my own spirit. The man had moved from physical darkness to light, and now from spiritual seeking to faith—and I noticed that the moment the world cast him out for Jesus’ sake was the very moment Jesus came to find him. Being thrown out of the synagogue had landed him at the feet of the Son of God. His words afterward lingered with me: “For judgment I came into this world, that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind.” The Pharisees nearby heard and asked if they were blind too. Jesus answered, “If you were blind, you would have no guilt; but now that you say, ‘We see,’ your guilt remains.” I understood then that the one thing that could shut a man out of this salvation was the proud certainty that he needed no healing.

Being with Jesus in those days felt like standing in the full glare of light—revealing, sometimes painful, yet full of hope. I saw how He brought sight to the blind in more ways than one, and how the same light exposed the blindness in proud hearts. My own eyes felt opened further, my loyalty to Him deepening even as the shadows around us in Jerusalem lengthened. I walked with Him through the courts and streets, storing these things carefully, knowing the path we were on was leading toward something far greater and more costly than I could yet fully grasp.

We lingered in Jerusalem after the healing of the blind man, the city still alive with the remnants of the Feast of Tabernacles. The courts of the Temple echoed with discussions and debates, and the air carried the mingled scents of incense, dust, and the faint sweetness of palm branches left from the celebrations. Tension hung over everything like a gathering cloud. Jesus continued to teach in the colonnades, and I stayed near Him, my senses alert to every shift in the mood of the crowd.

One day He spoke of Himself as the shepherd of the sheep. “Truly, truly, I say to you,” He began, His voice carrying clearly across the open space, “I am the door of the sheep. All who came before me are thieves and robbers, but the sheep did not listen to them. I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep.”

I listened with my whole being, feeling the weight and tenderness of those words. The image of a shepherd who would die for his flock stirred something deep within me, and at last it began to draw all His talk of suffering into focus. He had spoken again and again of being killed; now He told us why. He was not being overtaken by His enemies; He was a shepherd laying down His life, on purpose, between the flock and the wolf. I had seen shepherds on the hills—rugged, watchful men who knew each sheep by name—but I had never heard of one who meant to die so the sheep might live. Jesus spoke as One who knew us that intimately and would not flee when danger came. Some in the crowd murmured that He was mad or had a demon, while others defended Him, saying, “These are not the words of one who is demon-possessed. Can a demon open the eyes of the blind?” The division was growing sharper, like a blade slowly cutting through cloth. My own heart felt the strain—loyalty to Him burning brighter even as the opposition hardened around us.

Later, during the Feast of Dedication in winter, we were walking in the Temple, in Solomon’s Portico. The air was cooler now, and the light had a sharper quality as it fell across the stone columns. The people gathered around Him and asked directly, “How long will you keep us in suspense? If you are the Christ, tell us plainly.”
Jesus looked at them with steady sorrow and said, “I told you, and you do not believe. The works that I do in my Father’s name bear witness about me… I and the Father are one.”

The words fell with quiet power, yet they struck like lightning. I felt a holy thrill run through me, mingled with awe. He was claiming unity with the Father Himself—the Shepherd who would die for the sheep was no mere man hired to watch them, but God come down to do it. Some in the crowd picked up stones to throw at Him, their faces twisted with rage. Jesus asked them calmly, “I have shown you many good works from the Father; for which of them are you going to stone me?” They answered that it was for blasphemy, because He, being a man, was making Himself God. He responded with scripture and reminded them of His works, but they tried again to arrest Him. He slipped away from their hands, and we withdrew with Him across the Jordan to the place where John had first been baptizing.

There, many came to Him and believed. I sat with the others in the quieter countryside, the sound of the river nearby a constant, soothing murmur. Being away from the pressure of Jerusalem brought a measure of relief, yet my spirit remained watchful. The things I had seen and heard were accumulating like stones in a wall—each one strengthening my conviction that this was the Messiah, the Son of God. Even as the shadows lengthened over His path, I felt a deepening peace in simply being near Him, walking where He walked, listening to every word as if my life depended on it. And in many ways, I knew it did.

We stayed for some time in the region beyond the Jordan, in the place where John had first baptized. The land was quieter here, the river flowing steadily nearby with a low, constant voice that seemed to echo the baptizer’s old call to repentance. Fewer crowds pressed upon us, and the open air allowed space for deeper conversation. Jesus taught us privately in the evenings as we sat together, His voice calm and measured in the cooling twilight. I listened with an attentiveness that had grown sharper over the months, sensing that every word now carried extra weight, like provisions stored carefully before a long journey. It struck me that John had begun his work here pointing to the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world; now we had come full circle to the same riverbank, and that Lamb was about to do the very thing John had named.

In those weeks, as we moved from village to village through the country beyond the Jordan and up toward Judea, He taught without ceasing, and I held His words as a man holds water in cupped hands, afraid to lose a drop. When the crowds pressed in clamoring for a sign, He grew firm. “This generation is an evil generation. It seeks a sign, but no sign will be given it except the sign of Jonah. For as Jonah became a sign to the people of Nineveh, so will the Son of Man be to this generation.” I did not catch His meaning then, but I would: Jonah three days in the belly of the deep and brought up alive was the one sign He would give—His own death and rising, the very thing He kept promising. He spoke of the men of Nineveh and the queen of the South rising in the judgment, because they had repented and listened at far less than now stood before them. Then, more gently, He gestured to a lamp burning on its stand. “No one lights a lamp and puts it in a cellar, but on a stand, that those who enter may see the light. The eye is the lamp of the body. When your eye is healthy, your whole body is full of light.” One of the Pharisees invited Him to dine, and was astonished that He did not first wash. Jesus answered him without flinching, naming their careful tithing of mint and rue while they neglected justice and the love of God, their hunger for the best seats and the greetings of the marketplaces, the burdens they laid on others’ shoulders that they would not touch with a finger. The lawyers bristled, and from that hour they watched Him closely, waiting to catch Him in something He might say.

To us, His own, He turned with a quieter urgency. “Beware the leaven of the Pharisees, which is hypocrisy. Nothing is covered up that will not be revealed, and what you have whispered in private rooms will be proclaimed on the housetops.” He told us not to fear those who kill the body and after that can do nothing more, but to fear the One who has authority over body and soul together. Yet in the same breath He comforted us: not one sparrow is forgotten before God, and even the hairs of our heads are all numbered. “Everyone who acknowledges me before men, the Son of Man also will acknowledge before the angels of God.” And He promised that when we were dragged before rulers and authorities, the Holy Spirit would teach us in that very hour what we ought to say. I held those words close, not knowing then how soon I would need them, nor how badly I and the others would stumble before we learned to lean on them. There was comfort woven through the warning: the God who could weigh body and soul together was the same God who counted the sparrows and numbered my hairs, and a salvation held by a God like that could not slip out of His hands.

A man called out from the crowd, “Teacher, tell my brother to divide the inheritance with me.” Jesus refused to be made a judge over their property. “Take care, and be on your guard against all covetousness, for one’s life does not consist in the abundance of his possessions.” Then He told of a rich man whose land produced so plentifully that he resolved to tear down his barns and build larger ones, saying to his soul, “You have ample goods laid up for many years; relax, eat, drink, be merry.” But God said to him, “Fool!
