This night your soul is required of you, and the things you have prepared, whose will they be?” So it is, He said, with the one who lays up treasure for himself and is not rich toward God. And turning to us, He bade us not be anxious about our lives, what we would eat or what we would put on. “Consider the ravens: they neither sow nor reap nor gather into barns, and yet God feeds them. Consider the lilies, how they grow. If God so clothes the grass of the field, how much more will He clothe you. Seek His kingdom, and these things will be added to you.” The plain birds wheeling overhead and the wildflowers leaning along the path became, in His mouth, sermons I could not unsee afterward. He was teaching us to live as children whose Father could be trusted for everything—which was only possible, I realized, for those whose true treasure was no longer anything that this night’s death could take away.

He spoke often of readiness in those days. “Stay dressed for action and keep your lamps burning, like men waiting for their master to come home from the wedding feast, so that they may open the door at once when he knocks.” Blessed, He said, are the servants the master finds awake; but the servant who says in his heart, “My master is delayed,” and begins to beat the other servants and to eat and drink and get drunk, will be cut in pieces. To whom much is given, much will be required. He did not soften what His coming would cost. “I came to cast fire on the earth, and how I wish it were already kindled.” He spoke of a baptism He had still to undergo, and of how distressed He was until it was finished—and only much later did I understand He meant the flood of suffering that was rushing toward Him at Jerusalem. “Do you think I have come to give peace on earth? No, but rather division.” Households would be split, He warned, father against son and mother against daughter, for His sake. Then, turning to the crowds, He rebuked their dullness: they could see a cloud rising in the west and say a shower was coming, and feel the south wind and say there would be scorching heat, yet they could not interpret the present time. The warning settled over me like the chill that runs ahead of a storm.

Some told Him of Galileans whose blood Pilate had mingled with their sacrifices, as if such suffering marked the men as worse sinners than the rest. Jesus refused the cruel arithmetic. “Do you think they were worse offenders than all the others? No, I tell you; but unless you repent, you will all likewise perish.” He recalled the eighteen on whom the tower in Siloam had fallen, and said the same of them. Then He told of a man who had a fig tree planted in his vineyard and came seeking fruit on it for three years and found none. “Cut it down,” he told the keeper of the vineyard; “why should it use up the ground?” But the keeper pleaded, “Sir, let it alone this year also, until I dig around it and put on manure. Then if it should bear fruit next year, well and good; but if not, you can cut it down.” I understood that He was speaking of a patience that was real but would not last forever—and I heard in the keeper’s plea an echo of Jesus Himself, standing between the barren tree and the axe, buying it more time with His own care. I searched my own life for fruit, sobered that the danger was not only the gross sinner’s but mine: not worse offenders, but all alike in need of turning home before the season ran out.

On a Sabbath He taught in a synagogue where a woman had been bent over for eighteen years, unable to straighten herself at all. He called her to Him and said, “Woman, you are freed from your disability,” and laid His hands on her, and at once she stood up straight and began praising God. The ruler of the synagogue was indignant that He had healed on the Sabbath and told the people to come for healing on the other six days. But Jesus called him a hypocrite. “Does not each of you on the Sabbath untie his ox or his donkey and lead it away to water? And ought not this woman, a daughter of Abraham whom Satan has bound for eighteen long years, be loosed from this bond on the Sabbath day?” His adversaries were put to shame, and all the people rejoiced at the glorious things He did. It moved me that He called her a daughter of Abraham and named her bondage as Satan’s work; He had come to loose exactly such bonds, and would let no rule of men keep Him from setting a captive free. He likened the kingdom of God to a grain of mustard seed that a man sowed in his garden, which grew into a tree where the birds made their nests, and to leaven that a woman hid in three measures of flour until it was all leavened. Small, hidden beginnings, He seemed to say, with an end too large to measure—and I took heart that the rescue He was working, which looked so small and so opposed, would one day fill the whole earth.

Someone asked Him whether those who are saved would be few. He answered not with a number but with a door. “Strive to enter through the narrow door, for many, I tell you, will seek to enter and will not be able.” He warned that some would stand outside knocking, saying, “We ate and drank in your presence, and you taught in our streets,” only to hear, “I do not know where you come from.” People would come from east and west, from north and south, and recline at table in the kingdom of God, while some who counted themselves first would be last. I felt the urgency of it: the door was narrow, and it was open now, but it would not always be. That same hour certain Pharisees came warning Him to leave, for Herod wanted to kill Him. Jesus was unmoved. “Go and tell that fox that I cast out demons and perform cures today and tomorrow, and the third day I finish my course.” Then His voice bent with grief over the city that lay ahead of us. “O Jerusalem, Jerusalem, the city that kills the prophets and stones those sent to it—how often would I have gathered your children together as a hen gathers her brood under her wings, and you were not willing.” I had never heard such longing braided so tightly with such sorrow. The image undid me—the Lord of glory as a mother bird stretching her wings over her young to take the blow herself—and I wondered whether that was not exactly how He meant to gather us at last, by spreading Himself over us on something like outstretched wings.

He dined one Sabbath at the house of a ruler who belonged to the Pharisees, and they watched Him carefully. A man was there swollen with dropsy, and Jesus healed him and sent him away, then asked them which of them, if a son or an ox had fallen into a well on the Sabbath, would not at once pull him out. They could not answer Him. Noticing how the guests had chosen the places of honor, He counseled taking the lowest place instead, so the host might come and say, “Friend, move up higher,” for everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and the one who humbles himself will be exalted. And He told the host to invite not friends and rich neighbors who could repay him, but the poor, the crippled, the lame, and the blind. Then He told of a man who gave a great banquet and invited many, but when the hour came each of them began to make excuses—a field just bought, five yoke of oxen to examine, a wife newly married. In anger the master sent his servant into the streets and lanes to bring in the poor and crippled and blind and lame, and then to the highways and hedges to compel people to come in, that his house might be filled. “For none of those men who were invited shall taste my banquet.” I felt the warning aimed squarely at those of us who assumed our places at His table were secure—and I saw the gospel hidden in it too: the feast of God would not go unfilled for lack of worthy guests, but would be crowded instead with exactly the poor and broken and overlooked who knew they had no claim, dragged in joyfully off the roads by a host determined to fill His house.

Great crowds traveled with Him now, and He turned and gave them no easy welcome. “Whoever does not bear his own cross and come after me cannot be my disciple.” He asked which of them, intending to build a tower, would not first sit down and count the cost, whether he had enough to finish it, lest he lay a foundation and not be able to complete it, and all who saw it mock him. Or what king, marching out to meet another in war, does not first sit down and weigh whether with ten thousand he can meet the one coming against him with twenty thousand. “So therefore, any one of you who does not renounce all that he has cannot be my disciple. Salt is good, but if it has lost its taste, how shall its saltiness be restored?” The words thinned the crowd the way a hard climb thins a caravan, leaving behind those who only meant to travel a little way. I understood that He wanted followers who knew exactly what they were walking into—and the more I thought on it, the more I saw that He was asking nothing of us He was not Himself about to do in full, for He was the One walking ahead to bear the heaviest cross of all and renounce everything, even His life, for our sake.

The tax collectors and sinners were all drawing near to hear Him, and the Pharisees and the scribes grumbled, “This man receives sinners and eats with them.” So He answered them with a question that was really a mirror. What man among them, having a hundred sheep and losing one, does not leave the ninety-nine in the open country and go after the one until he finds it, and then lay it on his shoulders rejoicing and call his friends together to celebrate? Or what woman, having ten silver coins and losing one, does not light a lamp and sweep the house and search diligently until she finds it, and then call her neighbors to rejoice with her? “Just so, I tell you, there is joy before the angels of God over one sinner who repents.” Their grumble had been an accusation; He turned it into the very glory of God. I had spent my whole life among people taught to keep their distance from such sinners, and here was the Shepherd telling me that heaven does not wait at a safe distance for the lost to find their own way back—it goes out after the one, carries it home on its own shoulders, and throws a feast when it arrives. The receiving of sinners they sneered at was the deepest joy in heaven.

Then He told the story I have never been able to forget. A man had two sons, and the younger asked for his share of the estate, then gathered everything and journeyed into a far country, where he squandered it all in reckless living. When a severe famine arose and he had nothing, he hired himself out to feed pigs and longed to fill his belly with the pods they ate, and no one gave him anything. But he came to himself and said, “How many of my father’s hired servants have more than enough bread, while I perish here with hunger. I will arise and go to my father and say to him, Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you; I am no longer worthy to be called your son; treat me as one of your hired servants.” And while he was still a long way off, his father saw him and felt compassion and ran and fell on his neck and kissed him. Before the son could finish the confession he had rehearsed, the father called for the best robe, a ring for his hand, sandals for his feet, and the fattened calf, “for this my son was dead, and is alive again; he was lost, and is found.” But the older son, coming in from the field and hearing music and dancing, was angry and would not go in. His father came out and entreated him, and the son complained that he had served all these years and never disobeyed, yet was never given so much as a young goat to celebrate with his friends. The father’s answer hung in the cooling evening air. “Son, you are always with me, and all that is mine is yours. It was fitting to celebrate and be glad, for this your brother was dead, and is alive; he was lost, and is found.”

I looked at the tax collectors leaning in close, and at the scribes standing stiff at the edge of the crowd, and I understood there were two sons in the story for a reason. But it was the father I could not get past. I had imagined that a sinner crawling home should expect, at best, a cold acceptance and a long probation. Instead the father saw him while he was still far off—which meant he had been watching the road—and ran, an old man hitching up his robe and running like a fool to reach a ragged, pig-stinking boy and fall on his neck before a word of confession was even out. Here at last was the whole of what I had been slowly learning, gathered into one running figure: this is what God is like, and this is what He had come down to do—not to wait for the worthy, but to run toward the wretched, cut their rehearsed groveling short, and clothe them as sons. And I began to suspect, watching the father go out to plead even with the bitter older son, that there was no kind of lostness, neither the prodigal’s nor the prig’s, that this love would not leave the house to chase.

He told us, His own disciples, of a manager accused of wasting his master’s goods, who, about to be dismissed, shrewdly reduced the debts of his master’s debtors so they would receive him into their houses afterward. The master commended the dishonest manager for his shrewdness, and Jesus drew the lesson out sharply: “Make friends for yourselves by means of unrighteous wealth, so that when it fails they may receive you into the eternal dwellings.” The one faithful in very little is faithful also in much, and the one dishonest in very little is dishonest in much. “No servant can serve two masters. You cannot serve God and money.” The Pharisees, who loved money, heard all this and ridiculed Him; but He told them that what is exalted among men is an abomination in the sight of God. The Law and the Prophets, He said, were until John; since then the good news of the kingdom of God is preached, and everyone forces his way into it, yet it is easier for heaven and earth to pass away than for one dot of the Law to fail. I sat with that strange pairing—the kingdom flung open as good news to be pressed into, and not one stroke of the Law allowed to fall—and could not yet see how both could stand at once. Only later would I learn that they met in Him: that He would satisfy every dot of the Law in our place so that the door could be thrown open to sinners who could never satisfy it themselves.

There was a rich man, He said, clothed in purple and fine linen, who feasted sumptuously every day, and at his gate was laid a poor man named Lazarus, covered with sores, who longed to be fed with what fell from the rich man’s table, while even the dogs came and licked his sores. The poor man died and was carried by the angels to Abraham’s side; the rich man also died and was buried, and in torment he lifted up his eyes and saw Abraham far off and Lazarus beside him. He begged that Lazarus might dip the tip of his finger in water and cool his tongue, but Abraham answered that a great chasm had been fixed between them which none could cross, and that in his lifetime the rich man had received his good things while Lazarus received only evil. Then the rich man pleaded that Lazarus be sent to warn his five brothers. “They have Moses and the Prophets,” Abraham said; “let them hear them.” “No, father Abraham, but if someone goes to them from the dead, they will repent.” And the answer came back: “If they do not hear Moses and the Prophets, neither will they be convinced if someone should rise from the dead.” The story sobered me with how final the chasm became once death had fixed it, and how the time to cross it was now, on this side, while there was still a voice to heed. I did not know then how soon a man named Lazarus would in fact rise, nor how stubbornly the hard of heart would still refuse to believe—proof, in the end, that no wonder can save a heart that will not hear.

He warned us that temptations to sin are sure to come, but woe to the one through whom they come; it would be better to have a millstone hung around the neck and be cast into the sea than to cause one of these little ones to stumble. “Pay attention to yourselves. If your brother sins, rebuke him, and if he repents, forgive him; and if he sins against you seven times in the day, and turns to you seven times saying I repent, you must forgive him.” The apostles, staggered, said to the Lord, “Increase our faith.” He told them that faith like a grain of mustard seed could uproot a mulberry tree and plant it in the sea. Then He sobered us with a picture of plain service: when a servant has plowed or kept sheep and comes in from the field, his master does not thank him but expects to be served first; so we, when we have done all that we were commanded, should say, “We are unworthy servants; we have only done what was our duty.” It pressed the swelling pride out of me, that image of dusty, ordinary obedience that expects no applause. Even my best obedience earned God nothing; whatever I would ever receive from Him would be gift, never wage—and that, I was learning, was a relief and not a loss.

As we passed along between Samaria and Galilee, ten lepers met Him, standing at a distance as the law required, and lifted their voices together: “Jesus, Master, have mercy on us.” He looked at them and only said, “Go and show yourselves to the priests.” And as they went, they were cleansed—I watched the wonder break across their faces as the disease loosed its grip on their skin right there on the road. But just one of them, when he saw that he was healed, turned back, praising God with a loud voice, and fell on his face at Jesus’ feet, giving Him thanks; and he was a Samaritan. Jesus looked around almost in sorrow. “Were not ten cleansed? Where are the nine? Was no one found to return and give praise to God except this foreigner?” Then to the man at His feet He said, “Rise and go your way; your faith has made you well.” All ten were cleansed, but only the one who came back was told his faith had saved him—and again it was the outsider. I began to see there was a healing of the skin that anyone might receive and walk away from, and a deeper saving that came only to those who turned back to the Healer Himself in faith and thanks. The gratitude of the foreigner, and the silence of the nine who never returned, stayed with me long after the man had gone on his way.

When the Pharisees asked Him when the kingdom of God would come, He told them it would not come with signs to be observed, for the kingdom of God was already in their midst. But to us He spoke of the days of the Son of Man, which would be like the days of Noah and of Lot—people eating and drinking, marrying, buying and selling, planting and building—until the day judgment fell suddenly upon them. “Remember Lot’s wife,” He said. “Whoever seeks to preserve his life will lose it, and whoever loses his life will keep it.” To teach us to pray always and not lose heart, He told of a widow who kept coming to a judge who neither feared God nor respected man, until he granted her justice simply to be rid of her; and He asked how much more God will give justice to His elect who cry to Him day and night. And for some who trusted in their own righteousness and looked down on everyone else, He told of two men who went up to the temple to pray—a Pharisee who thanked God that he was not like other men, fasting and tithing, and a tax collector who stood far off and would not so much as lift his eyes, but beat his breast and said, “God, be merciful to me, a sinner.” “I tell you, this man went down to his house justified rather than the other. For everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, but the one who humbles himself will be exalted.” That word, justified, lodged in me. The man who brought God a ledger of his goodness went home with nothing; the man who brought only his sin and begged for mercy went home set right with God. I had spent years assuming heaven was won by the first kind of prayer, and Jesus had just told me it was answered only for the second.

When we crossed at last into the region of Judea, beyond the Jordan, crowds gathered to Him again, and the Pharisees came testing Him, asking whether it was lawful for a man to divorce his wife for any cause. He pointed them back past Moses to the beginning, to the Maker who from the start made them male and female, so that a man leaves father and mother and holds fast to his wife, and the two become one flesh. “What therefore God has joined together, let not man separate.” When they pressed Him about Moses’ certificate of divorce, He said Moses had allowed it because of their hardness of heart, but from the beginning it was not so. He spoke too of how jealously God watches over the little ones, repeating that whoever causes one of them to sin would be better off drowned in the depth of the sea, that their angels always behold the face of His Father, and that it is not the will of the Father that one of these little ones should perish. The weight He gave to the small and the overlooked rearranged something in the way I had been taught to see the world. If it was not the Father’s will that even one little one should perish, then the whole effort He was bending toward Jerusalem was of a piece with that will—a Shepherd going after every last sheep so that none would be lost.

People began bringing their little children to Him so that He might touch and bless them, and we, thinking to guard His time and strength, rebuked them. Jesus was indignant with us. “Let the little children come to me, and do not hinder them, for to such belongs the kingdom of God. Truly, I say to you, whoever does not receive the kingdom of God like a child shall not enter it.” Then He took them up in His arms, laid His hands on them, and blessed them one by one. I watched Him crouch down in the dust to a child’s small height, unhurried, attentive, and I was ashamed of how quickly I had counted them an interruption. The kingdom, it seemed, belonged most surely to those who could bring nothing in their hands but trust—who received it as a gift, the way a child receives, because they had no power to earn it and no thought of trying.

As He was setting out on the road, a young man ran up and knelt before Him. “Good Teacher, what must I do to inherit eternal life?” Jesus told him he knew the commandments, and the man said he had kept them all from his youth. Then Jesus, looking at him, loved him, and said, “You lack one thing: go, sell all that you have and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me.” The man’s face fell, and he went away sorrowful, for he had great possessions. I have never forgotten that Jesus loved him in the very moment of naming the one thing that held him back; the love and the hard word were not opposites. Jesus looked around at us and said, “How difficult it will be for those who have wealth to enter the kingdom of God. It is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter the kingdom of God.” We were astonished and asked who then could possibly be saved, and He answered, “What is impossible with man is possible with God.” The words settled something in me that had been unsettled since the beginning: no one—not the rich young man with his clean record, not I with all I had left behind—could thread himself through that needle by his own effort. Salvation was impossible for man and possible only for God, which meant it had to be, from first to last, a thing God did. Peter began to say that we had left everything to follow Him, and Jesus promised that no one who has left house or family or lands for His sake and the gospel’s will fail to receive a hundredfold now, along with persecutions, and in the age to come eternal life. “But many who are first will be last, and the last first.”

To explain that last saying He told of a master of a house who went out early in the morning to hire laborers for his vineyard, agreeing with them on a denarius for the day. He went out again at the third hour, and the sixth, and the ninth, and even at the eleventh hour, hiring those he still found standing idle. When evening came, he told his foreman to pay them all, beginning with the last hired, and each one received a denarius. Those hired first grumbled when they were paid the same, complaining that they had borne the burden of the day and the scorching heat. But the master answered one of them, “Friend, I am doing you no wrong. Did you not agree with me for a denarius? Take what belongs to you and go. Am I not allowed to do what I choose with what is my own? Or do you begrudge my generosity?” “So the last will be first, and the first last.” I felt the grumbling laborer’s complaint rise in my own chest, recognized in it the very voice of the older brother from the other story, and fell silent. The kingdom did not pay wages by the hour; it gave the same lavish gift to the latecomer and the lifelong laborer alike, because it ran on the master’s generosity, not on what we had earned—and the only thing that could spoil it was the pride that wanted to be paid what it deserved instead of given what it could never deserve.

As we went up the road toward Jerusalem, Jesus walked on ahead of us, and a kind of dread settled over those who followed. He took the Twelve aside and told them plainly what awaited Him: He would be delivered over to the chief priests and the scribes, condemned to death, and handed to the Gentiles to be mocked and flogged and crucified, and on the third day He would be raised. We did not grasp it; the meaning was hidden from us. And almost in the same breath, the mother of James and John came with her sons and asked that they might sit, one at His right hand and one at His left, in His kingdom. When the other ten heard it, they were indignant. So Jesus called us all together. “You know that the rulers of the Gentiles lord it over them, and their great ones exercise authority over them. It shall not be so among you. Whoever would be great among you must be your servant, and whoever would be first among you must be your slave, even as the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give His life as a ransom for many.” That word—ransom—broke over me like cold water and stayed with me longer than any other He spoke on that road. A ransom is the price paid to buy back a captive, to set a slave free. He was telling us, as plainly as He ever had, why He was walking toward death: not as a defeat that would befall Him, but as a price He had come to pay, His own life laid down in exchange for the many who could never buy their own freedom. That He could speak of His death and of our squabbling for greatness in a single breath unsettled and humbled me at once; we were grasping for thrones while He was on His way to purchase us with His blood.

We came to Jericho, and as He was leaving the city a great crowd went with Him. A blind beggar named Bartimaeus sat by the roadside, and when he heard that Jesus of Nazareth was passing by, he began to cry out, “Jesus, Son of David, have mercy on me!” Many rebuked him and told him to be silent, but he cried out all the louder, “Son of David, have mercy on me!” Jesus stopped and said, “Call him.” They told the man to take heart, that Jesus was calling him, and he threw off his cloak and sprang up and came. “What do you want me to do for you?” Jesus asked. “Rabbi, let me recover my sight.” And Jesus said, “Go your way; your faith has made you well.” At once he could see, and he followed Jesus on the road, glorifying God, and all the people who saw it gave praise as well. I had walked past a hundred beggars in my life without slowing; Jesus stopped the whole crowd for the one man no one else would hear. His was the right cry, I thought—not a claim of worth but a plea for mercy, flung out louder the more they tried to silence it—and it was answered. That was how a man came to Him: shouting for mercy over every voice that said to keep quiet.

In Jericho there was a man named Zacchaeus, a chief tax collector who was rich, and he wanted to see who Jesus was but could not on account of the crowd, for he was small in stature. So he ran on ahead and climbed up into a sycamore tree to see Him, since Jesus was about to pass that way. When He came to the place, Jesus looked up and said, “Zacchaeus, hurry and come down, for I must stay at your house today.” He came down at once and received Him joyfully, while the crowd grumbled that Jesus had gone in to be the guest of a sinner. But Zacchaeus stood and said to the Lord, “Behold, Lord, the half of my goods I give to the poor, and if I have defrauded anyone of anything, I restore it fourfold.” And Jesus said to him, “Today salvation has come to this house, since he also is a son of Abraham. For the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost.” I thought of Levi rising from his tax booth long before, and saw plainly that Jesus had never once stopped going after the very people the rest of us had quietly written off. Here at last, in one sentence, was the thing my whole journey with Him had been spelling out from the Jordan onward: the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost. Not to wait to be sought, but to seek; not to inspect the worthy, but to save the lost. Zacchaeus’ sudden open-handedness was not the price of his salvation but the first overflow of it—the prodigal’s robe, the forgiven woman’s tears, all over again, in a small rich man halfway down a tree.

Because we were now near Jerusalem and many supposed the kingdom of God was about to appear at once, He told us of a nobleman who went into a far country to receive for himself a kingdom and then return, leaving ten servants ten minas with the charge, “Engage in business until I come.” But his citizens hated him and sent word after him that they would not have this man reign over them. When he returned, having received the kingdom, he summoned the servants: the one who had made ten minas more was set over ten cities, and the one who made five over five; but the servant who had hidden his mina away in a cloth, excusing himself by calling his master a severe man, had even that one taken from him and given to the servant who had ten. “To everyone who has, more will be given; but from the one who has not, even what he has will be taken away.” And as for the citizens who would not have him reign, they were to be brought and judged before him. I heard in it a gentle correction of our eagerness—the kingdom was not going to burst into full glory the moment we reached the city; the King would first go away, and we would be left to trade faithfully on what He had entrusted until He returned. The parable fell heavily on all of us, so near the city now, and we went on, the journey narrowing toward Jerusalem, every step weighted with a hope and a fear I could no longer tell apart.

Then word came from Bethany, a village just outside Jerusalem. A messenger arrived, breathless and troubled, with news from Mary and Martha: “Lord, he whom you love is ill.” Lazarus. Our friend. I remembered him well—quiet, generous, a man whose home had often been a place of welcome. Jesus listened without immediate alarm. “This illness does not lead to death,” He said. “It is for the glory of God, so that the Son of God may be glorified through it.” We stayed two days longer where we were. I felt the tension among the disciples. Some wondered why we did not hurry. I myself wrestled with it—love and delay seemed at odds. Yet in His presence I was learning that His timing was never late, only purposeful, and that He sometimes let a darkness deepen precisely so that the deliverance, when it came, would leave no doubt about who had wrought it.

Finally He said, “Let us go to Judea again.” The others hesitated, reminding Him of the stones the Jews had recently taken up against Him. Jesus answered, “Are there not twelve hours in the day? If anyone walks in the day, he does not stumble, because he sees the light of this world. But if anyone walks in the night, he stumbles, because the light is not in him.” Then plainly: “Our friend Lazarus has fallen asleep. But I go to awaken him.” When we still did not fully understand, He said it clearly: “Lazarus has died, and for your sake I am glad that I was not there, so that you may believe. But let us go to him.” That He would walk knowingly back toward the men who wanted to kill Him, and do it to wake a dead friend, told me again that His own safety was never the thing He was guarding; He was spending Himself, step by step, on the lives of others.

We set out, the road climbing back toward Jerusalem. My heart was heavy with sorrow for our friends and with a growing unease about returning to danger. Yet walking beside Jesus steadied me. Thomas voiced what many of us felt when he said, “Let us also go, that we may die with him.” There was courage in those words, even if mixed with resignation. I felt it too—a willingness to follow even into the shadow.

When we arrived near Bethany, Lazarus had already been in the tomb four days. Martha came out to meet us first, her face drawn with grief but her faith still reaching. “Lord, if you had been here, my brother would not have died. But even now I know that whatever you ask from God, God will give you.” Jesus answered her with words that still echo in my memory: “I am the resurrection and the life. Whoever believes in me, though he die, yet shall he live, and everyone who lives and believes in me shall never die. Do you believe this?” Martha’s reply came with quiet strength: “Yes, Lord; I believe that you are the Christ, the Son of God, who is coming into the world.” He did not say He would bring resurrection or fetch life from somewhere else; He said He was the resurrection and the life. The thing every grieving heart longed for was not a power He wielded but a Person standing in front of Martha in the dust of the road—and I understood that to have Him was already to have life that death could not finally hold.

Mary soon followed, falling at His feet weeping. The sound of her sobs, joined by the mourning of friends who had come from Jerusalem, stirred deep compassion in Jesus. I saw His face change—troubled, moved with sorrow. He asked where they had laid him, and they led us to the tomb, a cave with a stone against the entrance. Jesus wept. The sight of His tears moved me profoundly. The One who knew He was about to raise Lazarus still wept at the grave—the Lord of life refusing to stand aloof from our grief, weeping with us before He delivered us. It was not distant power, but shared sorrow; He came down into the very ache of death before He undid it. Some around us whispered, “See how He loved him!”

Then came the moment I will never forget. Jesus told them to take away the stone. Martha hesitated, mentioning the odor after four days. But He reminded her gently of belief. When the stone was rolled aside, Jesus lifted His eyes to heaven and prayed: “Father, I thank you that you have heard me. I knew that you always hear me, but I said this on account of the people standing around, that they may believe that you sent me.” Then, with a loud voice that carried the full weight of authority, He cried out, “Lazarus, come out!”

The silence that followed was absolute. Then movement—shuffling, the sound of linen wrappings shifting. Lazarus emerged from the darkness of the tomb, bound hand and foot with strips of cloth, his face wrapped in a cloth. He was alive. Whole. The crowd gasped, some falling back in fear, others crying out in joy. Jesus said quietly, “Unbind him, and let him go.”

I stood transfixed, my legs weak beneath me. Tears streamed down my face unashamedly. Death had yielded once more, but this time it felt intensely personal. Our friend, cold in the tomb four days, now stood blinking in the sunlight. In that moment the glory Jesus had spoken of shone out, and the words at the roadside became flesh before my eyes: He was the resurrection and the life, and He had just proved it on a man four days dead. If His voice could call Lazarus out of a sealed tomb, then no grave—not even the one I sensed waiting for Him in Jerusalem—could be the end of the story. Yet even in the joy I sensed the gathering storm. This sign would not be ignored by those who opposed Him; the very raising of a dead man would, I would soon learn, hasten His own death. I remained close to Jesus, more committed than ever, knowing that whatever came next, I had seen enough to trust Him completely.

We stayed in Bethany for a short time after Lazarus emerged from the tomb, the village buzzing with wonder and disbelief. People came from Jerusalem and the surrounding towns to see both Jesus and Lazarus, the man who had been dead four days and now sat among us, eating and speaking in a voice still tinged with awe. I watched Lazarus closely—his movements careful at first, as though rediscovering his own body, his eyes often turning toward Jesus with quiet gratitude. The joy in that house was deep, yet I felt an undercurrent of danger. Word of the miracle spread like fire through dry grass, and I sensed the growing threat it posed; the clearest proof of His power to give life was becoming the very reason men resolved to take His.

Not many days later, reports reached us that the chief priests and Pharisees had gathered the Sanhedrin. They were troubled. “What are we to do?” they asked one another. “This man performs many signs. If we let Him go on like this, everyone will believe in Him, and the Romans will come and take away both our place and our nation.” Caiaphas, the high priest that year, spoke with cold calculation: “It is better for you that one man should die for the people, not that the whole nation should perish.” I felt a chill when I heard these words repeated by those who had been at the council. They did not understand that they were prophesying. He meant only to sacrifice an innocent man to protect their power; yet the words were truer than he knew, for Jesus would indeed die for the people—one man in the place of the many—and not for the nation only, but to gather into one the children of God scattered abroad. The deepest mystery of the whole plan had just been spoken aloud by the man who least believed it. From that day on, they plotted to put Him to death. Jesus therefore no longer walked openly among the Jews but went to the region near the wilderness, to a town called Ephraim, and stayed there with the disciples.

The days in Ephraim were quieter, the hills rugged and the air crisp. We rested, and Jesus continued teaching us in small, intimate moments. Yet even there, my sleep was sometimes restless. I would lie awake thinking of Lazarus walking out of the tomb, the grave clothes still wrapped around him, and then of the words spoken in the Sanhedrin. The joy and the shadow walked side by side—life pulled out of one grave, and a death being plotted for the One who had pulled it out.

When the Passover was at hand, Jesus left Ephraim and set His face once more toward Jerusalem. Many from the region went up to the city to purify themselves before the feast, and they looked for Him, wondering if He would come. The chief priests and Pharisees had given orders that anyone who knew where He was should report it, so that they might seize Him. As we drew near to Bethany again, six days before the Passover, a dinner was given in Jesus’ honor at the home of Simon the leper. Lazarus was there, reclining at the table with Him—a living testimony in the flesh. Martha served, as was her way. Then Mary took a pound of very costly ointment of pure nard, anointed Jesus’ feet, and wiped them with her hair. The fragrance filled the entire house—rich, heavy, and sweet.

I watched from across the room as the scent enveloped us. Judas Iscariot, one of the twelve, objected: “Why was this ointment not sold for three hundred denarii and given to the poor?” His words sounded righteous, but I sensed something false beneath them. Jesus defended Mary gently but firmly: “Leave her alone. She has kept this for the day of my burial. For the poor you always have with you, but you do not always have me.”

The words struck me deeply. Burial. He was speaking of His own death again, and this time the reality settled heavier in my chest. Mary had understood something the rest of us had not yet fully grasped—she had heard Him say He would die, and believed it, and so she lavished her treasure on Him now while she still could, anointing His body for the grave before the grave had even claimed it. Her act of extravagant love, poured out without calculation, humbled me. Nothing given to Him was ever truly wasted, however the careful world counted it; the only waste was holding back. I felt my own devotion tested—would I give so freely, so recklessly, to the One who was about to give His all for me?

The next day, the great crowd that had come to the feast heard that Jesus was coming to Jerusalem. They took branches of palm trees and went out to meet Him, crying out, “Hosanna! Blessed is He who comes in the name of the Lord, even the King of Israel!” Jesus found a young donkey and sat on it, just as it was written: “Fear not, daughter of Zion; behold, your king is coming, sitting on a donkey’s colt.” He came as a king, but not the kind the waving crowds wanted—no warhorse, no sword, only a borrowed colt; a King whose throne, I would soon see, was to be a cross, and whose conquest was to be His own death.

I walked near Him as we descended the Mount of Olives, the crowds swelling on every side. Their shouts rose like thunder, palm branches waving in the air, cloaks spread on the road before Him. My heart lifted with the praise, yet a sorrow lingered beneath it. I remembered His words about rejection and death. Many in the crowd had seen the raising of Lazarus and believed, but I knew not all hearts were true. As we approached the city, Jesus stopped and wept over Jerusalem. “Would that you, even you, had known on this day the things that make for peace! But now they are hidden from your eyes.” His tears on that day of triumph broke something open in me. While the city shouted His welcome, He wept for it, because He saw that the very peace it was singing about—the peace He had come to make—was being held out and refused. He had come to bring exactly what made for peace, at the cost of His own life, to a city that would spend that week putting Him to death.

We entered the city, the Temple courts filled with excitement and confusion. Some Pharisees in the crowd said to Him, “Teacher, rebuke your disciples.” Jesus replied, “I tell you, if these were silent, the very stones would cry out.”

That evening, as we returned to Bethany, the weight of all I had seen pressed upon me. The palms, the shouts, the tears, the fragrant ointment still lingering in my memory—everything pointed toward a climax I could not fully see, though I was beginning to feel its shape: that the King had come to His city to be crowned, and that the crowning would look like nothing any of us expected. I walked close to Jesus, my spirit quiet and attentive, more determined than ever to remain with Him through whatever darkness or glory lay ahead.

We returned to the city the next morning, the echoes of yesterday’s Hosannas still ringing faintly in my ears. The streets felt charged, as though the whole of Jerusalem held its breath. Jesus walked ahead of us toward the Temple with that same steady purpose I had come to recognize so well. As we entered the outer court once more, the familiar chaos met us—tables of money changers, merchants selling doves and oxen, the loud clink of coins and the lowing of animals filling the air.

I saw Jesus’ face change. A righteous fire kindled in His eyes, yet it was controlled, holy. He made a whip of cords as He had done years earlier, and began driving out the sellers. Tables overturned with heavy crashes, coins scattered across the stone pavement like rain. Animals bolted in confusion. His voice rang out clear and strong above the noise: “It is written, ‘My house shall be called a house of prayer,’ but you have made it a den of robbers!” I had stood in that court at the very beginning, when He first overturned these tables, and I understood it differently now. He was clearing His Father’s house of everything that stood between sinners and God—and within days He would offer His own body as the new and true temple, the one place where the whole world, Jew and Gentile alike, could finally come near to God in prayer.

I stood a short distance away, my heart pounding. The authority in His voice sent a tremor through me. Merchants scrambled to gather their goods, their faces flushed with anger and fear. The religious leaders watched from the edges, their expressions dark. Children in the court cried out, “Hosanna to the Son of David!” and the chief priests and scribes grew indignant. Jesus healed the blind and lame who came to Him there, and their joyful voices rose like incense. But the leaders’ opposition only deepened. I felt the growing divide like a crack widening in the ground beneath us. Being near Him in that moment filled me with both awe and unease—this was the same zeal I had witnessed at the first Passover, now burning brighter as the hour approached, as if He were cleansing the house one last time before offering Himself within it.

The following morning, as we left Bethany, Jesus was hungry. He approached a fig tree in full leaf along the path, but when He found no fruit on it, He said, “May no one ever eat fruit from you again.” The words were spoken quietly, yet with power. I noted it, but did not fully understand until later, when I saw the tree withered to its roots and remembered His parable of the fruitless fig tree spared one more year. A nation, like that tree, could be full of the leaves of religion and bear nothing for God—and the season for fruit would not last forever.

In the Temple courts that day, the chief priests, scribes, and elders confronted Him directly. “By what authority are you doing these things,” they demanded, “or who gave you this authority?” Jesus answered with a question of His own: “Was the baptism of John from heaven or from man? Answer me.” They argued among themselves, trapped by their own fear of the people. Finally they said, “We do not know.” Jesus replied, “Neither will I tell you by what authority I do these things.”

He then began teaching in parables. One struck me deeply—the story of the vineyard owner who planted a vineyard, leased it to tenants, and sent servants to collect fruit. The tenants beat and killed the servants, and finally killed the beloved son when he was sent. “What will the owner of the vineyard do?” Jesus asked. “He will come and destroy the tenants and give the vineyard to others.” I felt the weight of it, and a cold understanding crept over me: He was telling them, to their faces, exactly what they were about to do. He was the beloved son, sent last of all to a vineyard that had murdered every messenger before Him, and He knew they would kill Him too. Yet He spoke of the stone the builders rejected becoming the cornerstone, as if even His murder were folded into a plan that would build something the builders never imagined. The religious leaders knew He spoke of them. Their faces hardened with anger, yet they feared the crowd and did not seize Him.

They tried again later, sending some Pharisees and Herodians to trap Him with a question about taxes. “Is it lawful to pay taxes to Caesar, or not?” Jesus asked for a denarius, looked at the image, and answered, “Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s.” The wisdom and simplicity of His reply left them marveling and silent. I felt a quiet pride in Him, mixed with growing sorrow. They were not seeking truth; they were hunting for any reason to accuse—men circling the Lamb, looking for the pretext that would let them take Him to slaughter.

Later that day, Sadducees came with a question about the resurrection, presenting a complicated case of a woman married to seven brothers. Jesus answered with calm authority, quoting Scripture: “He is not God of the dead, but of the living.” The crowd was astonished at His teaching. A scribe then asked which commandment was greatest. Jesus replied, “The Lord our God is one Lord. And you shall love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your mind and with all your strength. The second is this: You shall love your neighbor as yourself. There is no other commandment greater than these.” The scribe agreed, and Jesus told him he was not far from the kingdom of God. For a moment, truth seemed to touch even some of His opponents. I marked the two commandments and felt their full weight—a whole-hearted love for God and neighbor that I had never once managed for a single day. Listening, I understood more sharply why I needed Him: the law named the love I owed and could not pay, and He was walking toward Jerusalem to pay it in my place.

As evening approached, Jesus sat opposite the treasury and watched people putting money in. Rich people gave large sums out of their abundance, but a poor widow came and put in two small copper coins. “Truly, I say to you,” He told us, “this poor widow has put in more than all of them. For they all contributed out of their abundance, but she out of her poverty has put in everything she had, all she had to live on.”

I felt the words pierce me. True giving, true worship, came from the heart’s deepest place. She had given not from her surplus but everything she had to live on—and it struck me, even then, that this was the very thing Jesus Himself was days from doing: not a portion offered out of abundance, but His whole life poured out down to the last. In the fading light of the Temple, with the sounds of the city beginning to quiet around us, I sensed the days of public teaching were drawing to a close. My spirit grew more solemn, holding tightly to every moment with Him, knowing the path we walked was leading toward a final, unavoidable hour.

We left the Temple courts as the sun dipped lower, casting long shadows across the white stones. I walked close behind Jesus, the image of that poor widow still vivid in my mind—her small, trembling hand dropping the two copper coins into the treasury with such quiet finality. Her face had held no bitterness, only simple devotion. Jesus’ words about her gift lingered in my chest like a warm coal. Everything she had. In that moment, I felt the gap between my own cautious offerings and the kind of wholehearted surrender she showed—the same surrender I was about to watch the Master make on a scale I could not yet imagine.

As we made our way out of the city and up the Mount of Olives, one of the disciples remarked on the grandeur of the Temple buildings—the massive stones, the gleaming gold, the towering architecture that spoke of permanence and glory. Jesus stopped and turned toward the city. His voice was quiet but carried a heavy solemnity: “Do you see these great buildings? There will not be left here one stone upon another that will not be thrown down.”

We sat down together on the slope overlooking the Temple, the evening light turning the city gold and orange. Peter, James, John, and I gathered closer, our hearts uneasy. “Tell us,” we asked, “when will these things be, and what will be the sign when all these things are about to be accomplished?”

Jesus began to teach us, and I listened with every part of me, feeling the weight of His words press down like the gathering dusk. He spoke of wars and rumors of wars, nation rising against nation, earthquakes and famines. “But the end is not yet,” He said. He warned of persecution, of being delivered up to councils and beaten in synagogues, of standing before governors and kings for His sake. “And the gospel must first be proclaimed to all nations.” That single line lifted my eyes above the coming troubles: whatever was about to happen to Him in Jerusalem, it would not bury the good news but launch it, until word of this Savior reached every nation on earth. My stomach tightened as He described brother betraying brother, children rising against parents, hatred because of His name. Yet He promised, “The one who endures to the end will be saved.”

He spoke of the abomination of desolation, of those in Judea fleeing to the mountains, of tribulation so great that if the days had not been cut short, no human being would be saved. I felt a holy fear settle over me as I looked out over Jerusalem, the city that had just welcomed Him with palms now appearing so fragile in the fading light. Then His voice softened with promise: “And then they will see the Son of Man coming in clouds with great power and glory. And then He will send out the angels and gather His elect from the four winds, from the ends of the earth to the ends of heaven.” The One soon to be seized and killed would come again in glory to gather His own from every corner of the earth—and I understood that the rescue He was about to accomplish would not be undone by the grave, but would reach its harvest on that day.

I sat in silence as the stars began to appear overhead, my hands resting on my knees. The contrast between the beauty of the night and the coming trials stirred a deep trembling inside me. I felt small, inadequate, yet strangely held. He spoke of the fig tree and the signs of summer, urging us to stay awake, to watch and pray. He told of servants entrusted with their master’s goods, of wise and foolish virgins waiting for the bridegroom, of a day when the Son of Man would separate the sheep from the goats and welcome the blessed of His Father into the kingdom prepared from the foundation of the world. “Heaven and earth will pass away,” He said, looking at each of us, “but my words will not pass away.”

As the night deepened, we returned to Bethany. The road was quiet now, our footsteps the only sound. My mind turned slowly over everything He had said, storing it like precious seed in fertile but troubled soil. The days of teaching in the Temple were ending. Something greater and more terrible was drawing near, and I knew I would need every word, every memory of His presence, to endure it. Yet walking beside Him, even in the gathering dark, I felt a quiet certainty: wherever this path led, I would not leave Him.

We returned quietly to Bethany that night, the path lit only by the moon and stars. The weight of Jesus’ words on the Mount of Olives pressed heavily upon me as I walked—wars, tribulations, the Temple stones thrown down, the Son of Man coming in glory. It all felt both distant and frighteningly near. My legs moved almost automatically while my mind turned slowly over everything, like a man trying to hold water in his hands. I felt small and unprepared, yet strangely anchored by His calm presence ahead of me on the road, the One who spoke of the end of all things as steadily as a shepherd describing the way home.

The next day, two days before Passover, we gathered again in the house of Simon the leper. The familiar scent of roasted lamb and herbs filled the air as preparations for the feast began. While we reclined at the table, Mary once more drew near to Jesus, the memory of her earlier costly gift still lingering over the room. The atmosphere was thick with unspoken tension. I could sense the shadow lengthening over us all—the feast of the Passover lamb drawing near, and the true Lamb reclining among us.

That same evening, Judas Iscariot slipped away. I noticed his absence but thought little of it at first—he often handled our money. Only later did I learn he had gone to the chief priests and offered to betray Jesus for thirty pieces of silver. The knowledge came like a slow knife. One of our own. One who had walked with us, seen the miracles, heard the teachings. It made the coming suffering feel more real, more personal—and it taught me a hard thing: a man could stand for years in the very presence of the Savior and still sell Him for silver, for nearness was never the same as faith.

On the first day of Unleavened Bread, when the Passover lamb was to be sacrificed, Jesus sent Peter and John ahead into the city. “Go into the city,” He told them, “and a man carrying a jar of water will meet you. Follow him, and wherever he enters, say to the master of the house, ‘The Teacher says, Where is my guest room, where I may eat the Passover with my disciples?’ He will show you a large upper room furnished and ready. Prepare there for us.” They went and found everything exactly as He had said. I marveled again at His complete knowledge of what was to come; the One who could order the smallest detail of the day was not being overtaken by events, but walking with open eyes into the hour He had chosen.

That evening we gathered in the upper room. The oil lamps cast a warm, flickering light on the walls. The table was set with the Passover elements—the bitter herbs, the unleavened bread, the wine. I reclined near Jesus, my heart full and uneasy. He looked around at each of us with deep affection, then did something that stunned us all.

He rose from the table, laid aside His outer garments, and tied a towel around His waist. He poured water into a basin and began to wash our feet, drying them with the towel. When He came to me, I felt the cool water on my dusty, calloused feet and His strong, gentle hands. The King of Israel—washing my feet like the lowliest servant. Shame and love flooded through me at once. When He reached Peter, Peter protested, “Lord, do you wash my feet?” Jesus answered, “What I am doing you do not understand now, but afterward you will know.” Peter declared he would never let Him do it. Jesus replied quietly, “If I do not wash you, you have no share with me.” Those words went deeper than the water. I understood, slowly, that the basin was a small picture of a far greater washing He was about to do; unless He cleansed us—not our feet only but our very souls, at a cost He had not yet named—we could have no share with Him at all. Peter then asked for his hands and head as well. Jesus’ humility broke something open inside me. If the Master stooped this low to serve, how could I ever again seek to be first?

After He had washed our feet and put on His garments, He sat down again and said, “Do you understand what I have done to you? You call me Teacher and Lord, and you are right, for so I am. If I then, your Lord and Teacher, have washed your feet, you also ought to wash one another’s feet. For I have given you an example, that you also should do just as I have done to you.”

The room was very still except for the soft crackle of the lamps. I felt tears welling up as His words sank in. Love expressed not in grand gestures alone, but in lowly, practical service. My spirit was both humbled and lifted. Being with Him in that upper room felt like standing on holy ground—intimate, tender, and shadowed by the knowledge that this might be our last meal together in this way.

Then Jesus grew troubled in spirit. “Truly, truly, I say to you,” He said, looking around the table, “one of you will betray me.” We looked at one another in shock and sorrow, each asking, “Is it I, Lord?” When He gave the dipped morsel to Judas, I saw something dark pass across Judas’ face. He left quickly into the night. None of us fully understood at the time, except that Jesus had told him to do quickly what he was going to do. Then, as we ate, Jesus took bread, gave thanks, broke it, and gave it to us. “Take, eat; this is my body, which is given for you. Do this in remembrance of me.” In the same way He took the cup after supper, gave thanks, and gave it to us, and we all drank from it. “This cup is the new covenant in my blood, which is poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins.” I held the broken bread in my hand and could scarcely breathe. Here was everything He had been telling us, gathered into bread and wine: the body given, the blood poured out, the forgiveness of sins. The bread of life He had spoken of in Capernaum, the ransom He had named on the road, the new covenant the prophets had promised—all of it was being placed into our very hands at a Passover table, on the night before He would become the Lamb. I ate and drank, and did not yet grasp it, yet I felt that I was receiving the heart of the whole matter.

In the quiet that followed, with Judas gone, Jesus spoke words of comfort and promise that I have held onto ever since. “Let not your hearts be troubled. Believe in God; believe also in me. In my Father’s house are many rooms. If it were not so, would I have told you that I go to prepare a place for you? And if I go and prepare a place for you, I will come again and will take you to myself, that where I am you may be also.” He was telling us why He had to leave: not abandonment, but preparation—His going to the cross and beyond it was the opening of the Father’s house to us, the making of a place where sinners could dwell with God forever. When Thomas asked the way, He answered, “I am the way, and the truth, and the life. No one comes to the Father except through me.” There was the whole of it: not a way He would teach us, but a way He Himself was; the only door home, and He was about to fling it open with His own body.

He spoke of the Holy Spirit, the Helper who would come. He called us His friends, not servants. He prayed for us. And He gave us a new commandment: “That you love one another: just as I have loved you, you also are to love one another. By this all people will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another.”

My heart burned within me as I listened. Love like His—selfless, sacrificial, serving. We were to love one another with the very love He was hours from proving on a cross. The night outside was dark, but in that upper room the light of His presence felt brighter than ever. I did not yet know how soon the darkness would come, but I knew I would follow Him through it.

We remained in the upper room as the night deepened, the oil lamps burning lower and casting long, flickering shadows across the walls. The air was heavy with the scent of wine, roasted herbs, and the lingering fragrance of the nard Mary had poured out earlier. Jesus looked at each of us with eyes full of both love and sorrow, as though He were already carrying the weight of what was coming.

“Little children,” He said gently, “yet a little while I am with you. You will seek me, and just as I said to the Jews, so now I also say to you, ‘Where I am going you cannot come.’” His words pierced me. I felt a sudden ache, like the first cold wind of winter. Where was He going that we could not follow? My hands tightened around the edge of the table as I leaned forward, hungry for every moment, every syllable. Only later would I understand: He was going where none of us could go for ourselves—down into death under the weight of our sin, to a place He had to enter alone precisely so that we would never have to.

Simon Peter, ever bold, asked, “Lord, where are you going?” Jesus answered him quietly, “Where I am going you cannot follow me now, but you will follow afterward.” Peter pressed further, his voice thick with emotion: “Lord, why can I not follow you now? I will lay down my life for you.” I saw Jesus’ face soften with compassion, yet there was pain there too. “Will you lay down your life for me? Truly, truly, I say to you, the rooster will not crow till you have denied me three times.”

The room fell into stunned silence. Peter’s face flushed with disbelief and hurt. I felt my own heart twist. If Peter—strong, impulsive Peter—could fall, what hope was there for the rest of us? And yet, even in foretelling the failure, Jesus had already provided for it; He had told Peter, "I have prayed for you that your faith may not fail, and when you have turned again, strengthen your brothers." The denial would not be the end of Peter, because the Savior would hold him through it. Jesus did not rebuke him harshly. Instead, He continued speaking words meant to strengthen us for the coming trial.

“I am the true vine, and my Father is the vinedresser. Every branch in me that does not bear fruit He takes away, and every branch that does bear fruit He prunes, that it may bear more fruit.” His voice was steady, almost tender, as if painting a picture we could hold onto. “Abide in me, and I in you. As the branch cannot bear fruit by itself, unless it abides in the vine, neither can you, unless you abide in me.” I felt those words sink into me like water into dry soil. Abiding. Remaining. Not striving in my own strength, but staying joined to Him and drawing all my life from Him—for, as He said plainly, apart from Him we could do nothing. The whole of the life He had been calling me into was here: not a list of duties to perform for God, but a union with Himself out of which everything else would grow. He warned us that the world would hate us as it hated Him, that we would be persecuted, even cast out of synagogues. Yet He promised the Helper—the Spirit of truth—who would come and guide us into all truth, convict the world of sin, and glorify Him. He told us our sorrow would turn to joy, like a woman’s anguish in birth forgotten in the joy of a child, and bade us take heart, for He had overcome the world.

My spirit trembled with both fear and hope as He spoke. He was preparing us, like a father speaking to his sons before a long journey. Then Jesus lifted His eyes to heaven and prayed—not just for us at the table, but for all who would believe through our word. “That they may all be one, just as you, Father, are in me, and I in you, that they also may be in us… I in them and you in me, that they may become perfectly one.” I listened with my head bowed, feeling as though I were overhearing something sacred, something eternal. To hear Him pray for people not yet born—for the ones who would believe because we told them what we had seen—made the whole sweep of His rescue suddenly vast: He was not saving the Twelve only, but gathering a countless family across all the years to come, and binding us into the very love the Father had for the Son. His love for us, for me, washed over me like a river. In that upper room, with the night pressing against the windows, I felt known, protected, and called into something far greater than myself.

After the prayer, Jesus rose. “Arise, let us go from here.” We followed Him out into the cool night air. The streets of Jerusalem were quiet now, the city mostly asleep. We crossed the Kidron Valley, the sound of our footsteps soft on the path, and came to a garden called Gethsemane on the slope of the Mount of Olives. Olive trees stood like silent witnesses in the moonlight, their leaves silver and still. Jesus told most of us to sit while He took Peter, James, and John a little farther. I stayed with the others at first, but the heaviness in the air drew me closer. I watched from a short distance as He fell to the ground and prayed with deep intensity, “Abba, Father, all things are possible for you. Remove this cup from me. Yet not what I will, but what you will.”

His voice carried such anguish that it tore at my heart. Sweat fell from Him like drops of blood onto the earth. I had seen Him calm storms and raise the dead without a tremor; now I watched Him shake before a cup He had not yet drunk. I did not understand then what that cup held, but I have since: it was the cup of God’s judgment against sin, the wrath I had earned, and He was steeling Himself to drink it to the dregs in my place. He could have refused it; instead He prayed, "not what I will, but what you will," and in that surrender the whole rescue hung. I wanted to go to Him, to comfort Him, but I felt paralyzed by the holiness of the moment. When He returned to us, He found us sleeping. “Could you not watch one hour?” He asked gently. The sorrow in His tone shamed me. I had failed even in this small thing while He bore the weight of the world alone. He prayed again, and again we slept. The third time He came, His voice was calm but resolute: “The hour has come. The Son of Man is betrayed into the hands of sinners. Rise, let us be going. See, my betrayer is at hand.”

In the distance, I heard the sound of approaching feet and the flickering of torches. My heart began to pound heavily. The long night of teaching and promise was ending, and the hour of darkness had arrived. I stood beside Him, my legs unsteady, yet determined to remain. Whatever came now, I would not leave His side.

We stood there among the olive trees as the torchlight drew nearer, casting dancing shadows through the branches. The night air was cool and heavy with the scent of crushed olives and damp earth. My heart hammered so loudly I could hear it in my ears. Judas appeared at the head of the crowd—soldiers from the chief priests and Pharisees, armed with swords and clubs, their faces grim in the flickering light. He stepped forward and kissed Jesus on the cheek. “Rabbi,” he said. The betrayal stung like a wound. One of our own. The man who had traveled with us, seen the miracles, shared our bread—now leading them to Him with the sign of friendship.

Jesus looked at Judas with sorrowful eyes and said, “Judas, would you betray the Son of Man with a kiss?” Then He turned to the armed men. “Whom do you seek?” They answered, “Jesus of Nazareth.” He replied calmly, “I am He.” At those words, the whole group drew back and fell to the ground. I stood frozen, watching powerful soldiers and officers sprawled on the dirt. The authority in His simple declaration was overwhelming. And it told me something I have never forgotten: no one was taking His life from Him. With a word He had laid them flat; He could have walked free through the lot of them. When Peter drew a sword and struck off the ear of the high priest’s servant, Jesus healed the man with a touch—mercy even to the one come to arrest Him—and told Peter to put away his sword, for the cup the Father had given Him, He would drink. He let them bind Him. The Lamb went willingly, because being seized was not His defeat but the very thing He had come to do. It filled me with a strange mixture of awe and fear, and the first dim understanding that everything happening to Him, He was allowing for our sake.

They rose again, more cautiously this time. Jesus spoke once more, “If you seek me, let these men go.” Even in the moment of His seizing, He was shielding us—securing our freedom as the price of His own surrender, the Shepherd stepping between the flock and the swords so that we could walk away. Peter, sudden and fierce, drew his sword and struck the high priest’s servant, cutting off his right ear. The man cried out in pain. Jesus immediately touched the servant’s ear and healed him—His last healing before the cross given to a man come to arrest Him. Then He turned to Peter with gentle rebuke: “Put your sword into its sheath. Shall I not drink the cup that the Father has given me?” I felt Peter’s shame as my own. We had been ready to fight, but Jesus chose another way—the way of obedience and sacrifice, refusing the rescue of the sword because only by drinking the cup could He rescue us.

They seized Him then, binding His hands. I followed at a distance with the others as they led Him back across the Kidron Valley toward the city. My legs felt heavy, my spirit reeling. The garden that had been a place of prayer was now the site of betrayal and arrest. I stayed close enough to see but far enough to avoid immediate danger, my heart torn between loyalty and fear. We went first to Annas, the father-in-law of Caiaphas the high priest. Questions were hurled at Jesus about His teaching and His disciples. He answered with quiet dignity: “I have spoken openly to the world. I have always taught in synagogues and in the Temple. Ask those who have heard me what I said to them.”

One of the officers struck Him across the face. The sound echoed sharply. I winced as if I had been hit myself. Jesus replied calmly, “If I have spoken wrongly, bear witness about the wrong; but if I have spoken rightly, why do you strike me?” The blow and His response burned into my memory. He stood there, bound yet regal, enduring injustice without retaliation—the innocent One already beginning to bear what the guilty deserved. My own courage felt small in comparison.

From Annas they took Him to Caiaphas, where the council had gathered through the night, hunting for a charge that would hold. I would learn the worst of what passed there soon enough; for now I clung to the edge of the courtyard, sick with dread, watching the torches move behind the walls.

As I stood warming myself by a fire in the high priest’s courtyard, a servant girl looked at me and said, “You also were with Jesus the Galilean.” Fear gripped me. I denied it. “I do not know what you mean.” Another pressed me, and again I denied. A third time, someone noted my accent: “Certainly you are one of them, for your accent betrays you.” This time I swore and cursed, “I do not know the man!” At that very moment, a rooster crowed. Jesus’ words from the upper room flooded back. I looked across the courtyard and caught His eye. He turned and looked at me. In that gaze was no anger—only sorrow and love. My heart broke. I went out and wept bitterly.

The night stretched on, dark and heavy. I had failed Him in the moment He needed me most. And yet, even as the shame crushed me, the look He had given me would not let me drown in it—there had been no condemnation in it, only a love that seemed to reach for me through my own denial. I understood, dimly, that if I were ever to be held, it would not be by the strength of my loyalty, which had just shattered, but by His love, which had not. I could not stay away. I would follow, even at a distance, through the trial and whatever came after. Though I had faltered, His love had not. The dawn was coming, and with it the hour of His greatest suffering. I remained, broken but still His.

I keep going back, in my memory, to what they did to Him in that council, for it is burned into me beyond forgetting. The Sanhedrin had assembled—chief priests, elders, and scribes—the room crowded, the air thick with the smell of oil lamps and incense. False witnesses were brought forward one after another, their testimonies twisted and contradictory. They spoke lies about Jesus destroying the Temple and rebuilding it in three days. These men were not seeking truth; they were hunting for any accusation that would stick. Jesus stood silent through much of it, His hands bound, His posture upright and calm—and I remembered the prophet’s words about a lamb led to the slaughter that opens not its mouth.

Finally the high priest stood and asked Him directly, his voice sharp with impatience: “Are you the Christ, the Son of the Blessed?” The room fell into a tense hush. Jesus looked at him steadily and answered with clear, solemn power: “I am. And you will see the Son of Man seated at the right hand of Power, and coming with the clouds of heaven.” He would not save His life with a denial as I had just saved mine; He confessed the truth that would cost Him everything.

A ripple of outrage swept through the council. Caiaphas tore his robes and cried out, “What further witnesses do we need? You have heard his blasphemy!” They condemned Him as deserving death. Then the mockery began. Some spat on Him. Others blindfolded Him, struck Him with their fists, and jeered, “Prophesy! Who is it that struck you?” The sounds of the blows and their mocking laughter cut through me like knives. This was the Man I had watched heal the sick with a touch, feed thousands, and speak words of eternal life. Now He endured their cruelty without resistance, taking in silence the scorn that should have fallen on guilty men like me. The humility and love in His silence overwhelmed me.

As the night wore on toward morning, the council bound Him more securely and prepared to take Him to Pilate, the Roman governor, since they did not have the authority to carry out a death sentence themselves. I followed as they moved through the dimly lit streets, the first faint gray of dawn touching the eastern sky. My legs felt heavy, my spirit bruised and weary. I had seen His glory on the mountain, heard His teachings in the upper room, watched Him pray in anguish in Gethsemane. And now this—the King of Israel being led like a lamb to slaughter, exactly as the Scriptures had foretold, exactly as He had told us He must.

Yet even in the darkness of that night, something held me. I could not turn away. The love and loyalty that had grown in me over these years refused to let me abandon Him completely, even as fear gnawed at the edges of my resolve. The path to Pilate’s headquarters lay ahead, and with it the final hours. I continued to follow, heart heavy but still fixed on Him—the One who had become my Teacher, my Lord, my everything.

I heard, in the midst of it all, what became of Judas. When he saw that Jesus was condemned, he was seized with remorse and came back to the chief priests with the thirty pieces of silver. “I have sinned,” he said, “by betraying innocent blood.” But they only answered, “What is that to us? See to it yourself.” He threw the silver down in the Temple and went away and hanged himself. The news landed on me with a strange and terrible weight, for I had denied the Lord that very night as surely as Judas had sold Him, and the difference between us was not the size of our sin. Judas carried his guilt back to the priests, who could do nothing with it but throw it in his face; he was sorry, bitterly sorry, yet he never carried that sorrow to the only One who could forgive it. I had wept as he despaired—but the look Jesus had given me across the courtyard had drawn my brokenness back toward Him rather than away. I saw then that remorse is not the same as repentance, and that even the worst betrayal is not beyond mercy for the one who will bring it home. The tragedy was not that Judas’s sin was too great to be forgiven, but that he died without ever turning to the One whose blood, even then, was being shed for sinners exactly like him.

We continued through the streets as the first gray light of dawn broke over the city. The guards led Jesus toward the Praetorium, the governor’s headquarters. My feet moved heavily on the stone pavement, each step echoing the growing dread in my chest. The air was cool and damp, carrying the faint smell of morning bread from nearby houses, but it felt wrong against the horror unfolding before me.

They brought Him before Pontius Pilate, the Roman governor. Pilate came out onto the pavement, his Roman cloak sharp and official in the early light. He looked at Jesus with a mixture of curiosity and irritation. “Are you the King of the Jews?” he asked. Jesus answered quietly, “Do you say this of your own accord, or did others say it to you?” Their exchange continued, Pilate questioning Him about His kingdom. Jesus replied with calm dignity: “My kingdom is not of this world. If my kingdom were of this world, my servants would have been fighting, that I might not be delivered over to the Jews. But my kingdom is not from the world.” He was a King, but His throne would not be seized by force or defended by swords; it would be won, I would soon see, by surrender.

I stood among the growing crowd at the edge of the courtyard, my heart swelling with strange pride and sorrow. Even bound and accused, He spoke with a royalty no earthly governor could claim. Pilate seemed unsettled. He found no guilt in Him and sought to release Jesus, but the chief priests and the crowd they had stirred shouted for Barabbas instead—a notorious rebel and murderer.
