Pilate asked again, “What shall I do with the man you call the King of the Jews?” They cried out louder, “Crucify him!” I watched a guilty man walk free that morning because an innocent One was condemned in his place, and the whole of it struck me later with terrible clarity: Barabbas was the first to be saved by the death of Jesus. The murderer went home to his family while the sinless One took the cross that had been meant for him—and I knew myself to be Barabbas, and so are we all.

Pilate, still hesitant, had Jesus scourged. I could not see everything clearly from where I stood, but I heard the sickening sound of the whip striking flesh again and again. When they brought Him back out, He was wearing a crown of thorns they had twisted and pressed onto His head, and a purple robe draped mockingly over His bleeding shoulders. Blood ran down His face. Pilate gestured toward Him and declared, “Behold the man!” The crowd roared back with hatred: “Crucify him! Crucify him!”

My knees nearly gave way. This was the Man I had followed for years—the One whose touch had healed the sick, whose words had fed my soul, whose glory I had seen on the mountain. Now He stood broken and bleeding before a hostile crowd. A deep, aching grief filled me, mixed with helpless anger at the injustice. Yet beneath it a stammering understanding was forming: the prophets had written that He would be wounded for our transgressions and crushed for our iniquities, that the punishment that brought us peace would be upon Him. I was watching it happen. Pilate washed his hands in a basin, declaring himself innocent of His blood, but still handed Jesus over to be crucified.

The soldiers took Him away to be prepared for execution. They stripped the purple robe from Him and put His own clothes back on His torn back. A heavy wooden crossbeam was laid across His shoulders. I followed as they led Him out of the city toward the place called Golgotha, the Skull. The road was rough, and Jesus stumbled under the weight. At one point, the soldiers seized a man named Simon from Cyrene who was coming in from the country and forced him to carry the cross behind Jesus. He was led outside the city walls to die, I thought—cast out, as the sin offering was carried outside the camp and burned, bearing away what defiled the people.

A large crowd followed, including many women who mourned and lamented for Him. Jesus turned to them and said, “Daughters of Jerusalem, do not weep for me, but weep for yourselves and for your children.” His concern for them, even in His own suffering, pierced me deeply. How could One so selfless still think of others while walking toward His death? Even here, bleeding toward the cross, He was the Shepherd, grieving for the sheep more than for Himself.

We reached the hill called Golgotha. The soldiers offered Him wine mixed with myrrh to dull the pain, but He refused it. They laid Him on the cross and drove the nails through His hands and feet. The sound of the hammer striking metal echoed horribly in the morning air. I stood at a distance with the others, my body shaking, tears streaming down my face. They lifted the cross into place between two thieves. Above His head they placed a sign: “Jesus of Nazareth, the King of the Jews.” He was numbered with the transgressors, lifted up between two criminals—and I remembered His words to Nicodemus long ago, that as Moses lifted the serpent in the wilderness, so the Son of Man must be lifted up, that whoever looked to Him might live. Now He was lifted up, and the looking and the living could begin.

As He hung there, the soldiers divided His garments and cast lots for His tunic. The chief priests and scribes mocked Him from below: “He saved others; let Him save Himself if He is the Christ of God!” Even one of the criminals crucified beside Him railed against Him. But the other rebuked him and turned to Jesus with humble faith: “Jesus, remember me when you come into your kingdom.” Jesus answered him with tenderness, “Truly, I say to you, today you will be with me in paradise.” It undid me, even in my grief. They had jeered that He could not save Himself—and they were right, for to save us He would not save Himself. And there, in His dying hour, with nailed hands and no strength left, He was still saving: a condemned criminal who could do no good work, offer no payment, only gasp out a plea for mercy, was promised paradise that very day. I had watched Him receive sinners for three years; His very last act before death was to receive one more.

I remained there through the long hours, watching as darkness covered the land from the sixth hour to the ninth. At the ninth hour, Jesus cried out with a loud voice, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” The cry tore through me. He who had always called God Father now cried out as one forsaken—and slowly, in the years since, I have understood why: He was bearing my forsakenness, drinking to the dregs the cup of being cut off from God that my sins had earned, so that I would never have to be forsaken. Then He cried, “It is finished,” and finally, “Father, into your hands I commit my spirit.” With that, He bowed His head and gave up His spirit. It is finished—not He is finished, but the work, the debt, the ransom, all of it paid in full and complete. And in that same moment, we were told, the great curtain of the Temple was torn in two from top to bottom, the veil that had shut sinners out of the Holy Place ripped open by no human hand. The way to God He had spoken of was thrown wide at the instant He died.

The earth shook. The centurion standing by said in awe, “Truly this man was the Son of God.” I stood there, numb with grief, my heart torn open. The One I had followed, loved, and believed in had died. Yet even in the crushing sorrow, something deeper stirred—a quiet hope I could not yet name. I had been with Him to the end. And somehow, I knew this was not truly the end. A Roman executioner had seen what the council could not, and even at the foot of the cross the gathering of believers had already begun.

We remained at the foot of the cross as the darkness that had covered the land began to lift. The air felt heavy and still, as though all creation held its breath. I stood with John and a few others at a distance, my eyes fixed on Jesus’ lifeless body hanging there between the two thieves. His head was bowed, His body limp and bloodied. The sight tore at me in a way no words can fully describe. This was the Man who had walked with us, taught us, healed the sick, fed the multitudes, and revealed the glory of God. Now He was gone. A profound emptiness settled in my chest, like a deep well with no bottom. I did not yet understand that the darkest thing I had ever witnessed was the very heart of the rescue—that He was never more the Savior than in the hour He seemed most defeated.

Joseph of Arimathea, a respected member of the council who had secretly been a disciple of Jesus, went boldly to Pilate and asked for the body. Pilate granted it, surprised that Jesus had died so quickly. Joseph came with Nicodemus, the one who had come to Jesus by night long ago. Together they took the body down with careful reverence. I helped where I could, my hands trembling as we lowered Him. The weight of His lifeless form pressed not only on my arms but on my soul. They wrapped Him in clean linen cloths with spices—myrrh and aloes—according to the burial custom of the Jews. The fragrance was strong and sweet, almost overwhelming in its contrast to the horror of the day; I thought of Mary’s ointment at Bethany, poured out, He had said, for the day of His burial, and saw that she had understood before any of us. They laid Him in Joseph’s own new tomb, cut into the rock nearby, and rolled a great stone against the entrance. The women who had followed Him from Galilee—Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James, and Salome—watched where He was laid. Their quiet weeping mingled with the fading light as the Sabbath drew near.

We returned to the city as evening fell, our steps slow and heavy. The streets felt strangely empty now, the earlier crowds dispersed. I found a place to rest, but sleep evaded me. My mind replayed every moment: the upper room, the garden, the trials, the scourging, the nails. Grief pressed on me like a physical weight. All our hopes seemed buried with Him in that tomb. Yet even in the darkness of that night, small flickers of memory returned—the times He had spoken of rising again on the third day, the way He had called Lazarus out of the grave, the sign of Jonah, the temple He would raise in three days. I dared not hope too much, but neither could I fully despair. Something in me refused to let go completely, as if His own words were keeping a small lamp lit against the dark.

The Sabbath passed in quiet sorrow. We rested as the law required, but our hearts were far from rest. I stayed mostly with the others, speaking little, each of us lost in our own thoughts and memories. The women prepared spices and ointments to anoint His body after the Sabbath, their devotion unwavering even in grief.

Then came the first day of the week, very early in the morning while it was still dark. I was awakened by urgent voices. Mary Magdalene had come running, her face a mixture of fear and astonishment. “They have taken the Lord out of the tomb,” she said breathlessly, “and we do not know where they have laid Him.” Peter and I ran together to the tomb. I outran him and reached it first. Stooping to look in, I saw the linen cloths lying there, but the body was gone. Peter arrived and went inside. The face cloth that had been on Jesus’ head was folded up in a place by itself. We stood there in the dim light of the tomb, the stone rolled away, and something began to stir in me—a dawning realization mixed with disbelief. The grave clothes lay undisturbed, as if His body had simply passed out of them; no thief steals a corpse and leaves the wrappings folded. He was not there. And then I remembered everything He had said, and I believed.

We returned to the others, our minds racing, but the full wonder had not yet broken over me. Later that same day, as some of us gathered behind closed doors for fear of the Jews, Jesus Himself stood among us. “Peace be with you,” He said. My heart nearly stopped. It was Him—alive, bearing the wounds in His hands and side. Joy flooded through me like a river breaking through a dam. He showed us His hands and His side, and we rejoiced with a gladness deeper than any we had known before. The grief of the cross gave way to a wonder that filled every part of me. Death had not held Him. And I understood, all at once, what the whole journey had been moving toward: the cross had not been a defeat that the resurrection reversed, but a victory that the resurrection proclaimed. The ransom had been paid and accepted; the debt was truly finished; the forsakenness was over; the Lamb who was slain was standing in the room, alive forevermore, and the wounds He carried were now the very proof and seal of our salvation.

In the days that followed, He appeared to us again and again—by the sea where He restored Peter, on the mountain where He commissioned us, in the upper room where He opened our minds to understand the Scriptures. He walked us through Moses and the Prophets and showed how all of it had been pointing to this: that the Christ should suffer and rise, and that forgiveness of sins should be proclaimed in His name to all nations. Everything I had glimpsed in pieces over three years—the Lamb of God, the bread of life, the good shepherd laying down His life, the ransom for many, the seeking of the lost—now stood together in the full light, and I saw it had been one plan all along. My spirit was remade in those encounters. The road that had led through Gethsemane and Golgotha had not ended in darkness, but in glorious light.

We remained with Him for forty days after His resurrection, and those days were unlike any that had come before. He appeared to us at different times and in different places, always bringing peace and deeper understanding. Sometimes He would suddenly stand among us when the doors were shut, and we would startle at first, our hearts leaping with joy once we recognized Him. He ate with us—broiled fish and honeycomb—to show that He was not a spirit but truly risen in body. I touched His hands and His side where the wounds remained, and the feel of them beneath my fingers filled me with awe. The scars were real, yet they no longer spoke of defeat. They spoke of victory—the marks of the price He had paid, carried now in a body that could never die again.

One morning by the Sea of Galilee, we had fished all night and caught nothing. As dawn broke, a figure stood on the shore and called out, “Children, do you have any fish?” We said no. He told us to cast the net on the right side of the boat. When we did, the net filled so full we could hardly drag it in. John recognized Him first: “It is the Lord!” Peter jumped into the water and swam to shore. There on the beach, Jesus had prepared a charcoal fire with fish and bread. We ate together in the early morning light, the sound of gentle waves on the pebbles mixing with the crackle of the fire. After breakfast, Jesus restored Peter with three gentle questions of love, undoing his three denials by another charcoal fire. I watched with a full heart, feeling my own failures and restorations in Peter’s—for I, too, had denied Him in my heart that night, and I, too, was being gathered back not by my faithfulness but by His. This was how He treated those who had fallen: not casting them off, but seeking them out and giving them work to do.

On a mountain in Galilee where He had directed us, Jesus met with more than five hundred brothers and sisters at once. He stood before us all, alive and radiant, and gave us the commission that still burns in my soul: “All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me. Go therefore and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, teaching them to observe all that I have commanded you. And behold, I am with you always, to the end of the age.”

His voice carried across the hillside with quiet power. I felt the weight and the wonder of those words settle deep within me. We were no longer just followers—we were sent ones, charged to carry to every nation the very rescue I had watched unfold from the Jordan to the empty tomb. The plan had never been for the saving to stop with us; we had been gathered in order to be sent. A holy fear and excitement stirred in my chest. I looked at His face, the same face I had first seen years ago by the river, and knew that everything had been leading to this.

Then came the day of His ascension. He led us out to the Mount of Olives, near Bethany. The air was clear, the sky wide and blue above the olive trees. He lifted His hands and blessed us. As He did, He was lifted up before our eyes, and a cloud took Him out of our sight. We stood there gazing upward, our hearts full to overflowing. Two men in white robes appeared beside us and said, “Men of Galilee, why do you stand looking into heaven? This Jesus, who was taken up from you into heaven, will come in the same way as you saw Him go into heaven.”

We returned to Jerusalem with great joy, as He had commanded us to wait for the promise of the Father. Those final moments with Him remain burned into my memory—the blessing, the cloud, the empty place where He had stood. I had walked with Him from the very beginning, from the banks of the Jordan to the cross and beyond the empty tomb. I had seen His glory, felt His compassion, heard His words of life, and witnessed His victory over death. And I had finally understood what John the Baptist had meant on the first day, when he pointed and cried, “Behold, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world.” It had taken me all those years, and a cross, and an empty tomb, to grasp it; but I grasped it now.

And now, though He is no longer walking visibly beside us, I know He is with us still, just as He promised. The light that first drew me to Him has never gone out. It burns brighter than ever in my heart, and I will spend the rest of my days telling what I have seen and heard—the story of the Word who became flesh and dwelt among us, full of grace and truth; the story of how God came to seek and to save the lost, and did not stop until the work was finished.
